According to this principle, the Great Vows universally encompass all; when Śākyamuni attained fruition, he praised this principle extensively with his broad tongue.
Thus, the great sages and supreme saints all unfurled their literary talents to form an oath, and the eminent masters of awakened virtue exhausted their brushes to compose these pledges.

If one seeks that which is most simple and most direct, nothing compares to faith and aspiration while single-mindedly upholding the Name.
For this reason, although the three Pure Land sutras are practiced together, the ancients exclusively took the *Amitābha Sūtra* as their daily recitation.

Is it not because this single method of upholding the Name universally accommodates the three capacities, encompasses both phenomena and principle without omission, and unifies all teachings and schools without exception—truly inconceivable?

This *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) comprehensively addresses all inquiries regarding the Pure Land school, upholds the fundamental principles of the Great Path to Bodhi, severs doubt, and engenders faith;
its merit is most immense. Shandao said: "Cultivating other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish;
only this dharma-gate allows for swift transcendence of birth and death. For those who practice it exclusively, ten out of ten will be reborn [in the Pure Land]. Master Fazhao was moved by Mañjuśrī.
He said: "Now that you are recollecting the Buddha, this is precisely the right time. You should know that the practice of *nien-fo* (recollection of the Buddha) is the sovereign of all dharmas.
As the Sun of Wisdom, Guanshiyin also said: "You should know that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land surpasses all other practices.
Since these two Great Beings are both the eldest sons of the Dharma King, and they have personally transmitted the Dharma-gate of *nien-fo* with such earnestness, how could one not believe it?
Feixi, Yongming, Siming, Cizhao, Yudantuo, Tianru, Miaoye, Chushi, Youxi, and others—these were the patriarchs who transmitted the lineage and the holy masters who expounded the teachings.

They engage in hollow boasting. Some say that reciting the Buddha’s name with a distracted mind is of no benefit; others say that one must recite with single-mindedness and without confusion;
still others say that one must investigate who it is that recites. When questioned about their faith and vow, they know nothing at all. How lamentable this is!

The King of Wish-Fulfilling Jewels, when encountered by such people as these, becomes mere rubble. For this reason, I have set forth the exposition on faith, aspiration, and the recitation of the Name through the nine grades;
practitioners should diligently study it. Furthermore, it is said: "Whether one attains birth [in the Pure Land] or not depends entirely upon the presence or absence of faith and aspiration;

How could one envy a vague semblance of understanding? Sheng'an said: 'To briefly hold the sacred name for a moment is superior to practicing charity for a hundred years.'"

A single arousal of the great mind surpasses eons of gradual cultivation. Upon thorough awakening, it is said: "The single gate of the Pure Land is the most fundamentally sought-after door of enlightenment;
at the end, it does not require the development of wisdom, nor the repentance of karma, nor the severing of afflictions.

It is the ultimate in economy and essentiality, the ultimate in directness and swiftness. When one enters its realization, it is the ultimate in vastness and the ultimate in finality. Thus, this is the Essential Explanation.
It is said: "One utterance of 'Namu Amida Butsu' is the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment) attained by our original teacher Śākyamuni in this world of five turbidities.
Now, this fruition of awakening is bestowed in its entirety upon sentient beings in this defiled and evil age.
This is the realm traversed by all Buddhas; it can be fully realized only by Buddha after Buddha, and is not [the domain] of the nine realms."

This is what can be believed and understood through one’s own efforts, as described above. All of this follows the sincere words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; it is not a matter of venturing into speculative discourse.

I have extracted those passages whose terminology is clear, whose meaning is manifest, and which are most essential, compiling them into a single volume for the purpose of solemn recitation morning and evening, so that one may be reminded at every moment as if hearing the Dharma directly from the lips of the Master.
Without daring to harbor any doubt or hesitation, I have entitled this work: *The Essential Teachings of the Lotus School*.
Read. My own karmic obstacles are deep and heavy; my turbid wisdom surges like waves. Without single-minded cultivation of one practice, it is difficult to escape birth and death.
Without relying upon the sacred teachings, the stages of faith and aspiration are difficult to ascend. Moreover, the time since the Sage departed is remote, and heterodox winds rise in competition;

those who practice the correct path are frequently deluded and disturbed. For this reason, one must read this book, and only then will one certainly be born in the Pure Land. I am ashamed of my own humble views.
I am narrow-minded and inferior; how would I dare to present this to my esteemed friends? I have done so only to urge myself on and to serve as a contract for rebirth in the Pure Land.

Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of...
The bhikṣus numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty, all of whom were great arhats renowned to the world.
Among them were the elders Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Mahākātyāyana,
Mahākauṣṭhila, Revata, Cūḍapanthaka, Nanda, Ānanda, Rāhula, and Kapphiṇa.

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Śāriputra: "From here, passing through a hundred thousand billion buddha-fields to the west, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a Buddha, titled Amitābha, who currently resides there."
He preached the Dharma, saying: "Śāriputra, for what reason is that land called 'Utmost Bliss' (Sukhāvatī)?
Because the sentient beings in that country have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is named 'Utmost Bliss.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the land of Utmost Bliss is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all made of the four precious substances. Therefore, that..."
The land is named Sukhāvatī. Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Sukhāvatī there is ground of the seven treasures, filled with water of eight virtues.
The bottom of the ponds is entirely covered with golden sand. The stairways on all four sides are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Above them are multi-storied pavilions, likewise made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, and red pearl.
It is adorned with pearls and agate. The lotuses in the ponds are as large as chariot wheels;

those that are blue emit a blue light, those that are yellow emit a yellow light, those that are red emit a red light, and those that are white emit a white light—subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss is thus perfected with such meritorious adornments. Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, it is constantly...
The heavens provide music, and the ground is made of gold. Six times throughout the day and night, it rains celestial *māndārava* flowers.
The sentient beings of that land regularly at dawn each take a robe-sack filled with various wonderful flowers to make offerings to hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas in other directions.
At the time of eating, he returned to his own country to eat and perform walking meditation.
Śāriputra, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is adorned with such accomplished merits and graces.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that land constantly has various wonderful birds of diverse colors: white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śāris, kalaviṅkas, and *saṃjīva* (co-life) birds.
These various birds, throughout the six periods of day and night, produce harmonious and elegant sounds.

Those sounds eloquently expound upon the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and such dharmas as these. When the sentient beings of that land hear these sounds, they [attain understanding].
They all constantly mind the Buddha, mind the Dharma, and mind the Saṅgha. Śāriputra, do not say that these birds are truly born as a result of their karmic retribution for sins.
Why is this? In that Buddha-land, there are no three evil realms of existence.
Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, even the names of the evil realms do not exist, let alone their actual presence. All these various birds are [emanations of] Amitābha.
The Buddha, wishing to cause the sound of the Dharma to flow forth, performs transformations.

Śāriputra, in that buddha-land, when a gentle breeze stirs the rows of jewel trees and the jeweled nets, they produce a subtle and wondrous sound, like the music of hundreds of thousands of kinds of instruments.
They act simultaneously; those who hear this sound naturally give rise to thoughts of mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
Śāriputra, that buddha-land is thus adorned with such perfected merits. Śāriputra, what do you think?
For what reason is that buddha named Amitābha? Śāriputra, the light of that buddha is immeasurable.
He illumines the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction; for this reason, he is named Amitābha.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; therefore, he is named Amitāyus.
Śāriputra, since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have now passed.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats; they cannot be known by means of calculation.
The assembly of bodhisattvas is likewise so. Śāriputra, that Buddha’s land is thus perfected.
This is the adornment of merit. Furthermore, Śāriputra, those beings who are born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
Among them, there are many who are in their last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), so numerous that they cannot be known by calculation;
they can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). Śāriputra, when sentient beings hear...
Such a person should make this vow: "May I be born in that land. Why is this? It is because one shall be able to dwell together with such superior and virtuous people in that single place.
Śāriputra, it is not by means of few roots of goodness, merit, or karmic conditions that one can be born in that land.
Śāriputra, if there are good men or good women who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, hold fast to it...
If one holds the name for one day, or two days, or three days, or four days, or five days, or six days, or seven days,
with single-mindedness and without distraction, then at the time of that person’s death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy beings,
will appear before them. At the moment of death, this person’s mind will not be inverted, and they will immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land of Amitābha.

In the east, there are also Buddhas such as Akṣobhya, Sumerukūṭa, Mahāsumeru, Sumeruprabhāsa, and Gadgadasvara—Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.

In the thousandfold world system, he spoke these truthful words:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas.
Śāriputra, in the southern direction there are the Buddhas Candrasūryapradīpa, Yaśaḥprabha, Mahārciskandha, Merupradīpa, and Anantavīrya. As...

"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, which is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Śāriputra, in the western world, there is...

This is the *Sūtra on the Praise of the Inconceivable Merit and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas*.

Śāriputra, in the worlds of the northern direction, there are the Buddha Flame-Shoulder, the Buddha Most Supreme Sound, the Buddha Unassailable, the Buddha Sun-Born, the Buddha Net-Luminosity, and other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Each, in their respective lands, extends the mark of a broad and long tongue until it covers [the entire world].
It covered the trichiliocosm. He spoke these words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe this Sutra on the Praise of Inconceivable Merit, which is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
Śāriputra, in the world-systems below, there are Buddhas named Siṃha, Yaśas, Prabhāsa, Dharma, Dharmadhvaja, and Dharmadhara.

In this manner, as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River each, within their respective lands, extend their broad and long tongues, covering the entire trichiliocosm, and speak words of truth:
"You sentient beings, you should believe in this *Sūtra on the Merit of Inconceivable Praise and the Protection and Mindfulness of All Buddhas*. Śāriputra, in the world-system above...

[His] marks completely cover the trichiliocosm. He speaks words of truth:

all these sons and daughters of good family shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas,
and they shall all attain non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, Śāriputra, you all...
"You should believe and accept my words, as well as what has been spoken by all the Buddhas.

Śāriputra, if there are those who have already made a vow, are now making a vow, or will make a vow, desiring to be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha—all such persons shall attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Whether they have already been born in that land,"
In this life or in future lives— for this reason, Śāriputra, any son of good family or daughter of good family who possesses faith should make a vow to be born in that land. Śāriputra,
just as I now praise the inconceivable merits of all Buddhas, so too do those Buddhas praise my inconceivable merits.
And he spoke these words: "Śākyamuni Buddha is able to perform a most difficult and rare feat;

he is able, within the five turbidities of the Sahā world—the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of views, the turbidity of afflictions, the turbidity of sentient beings, and the turbidity of life—to [act] amidst such a degenerate age."
I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and, for the sake of all sentient beings, have preached this Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe.
Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task:
having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I preach this Dharma that is difficult to believe for the sake of the entire world.

"This is most difficult. When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all those in the world—devas, humans, asuras, and others—hearing what the Buddha had said, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated, and departed.
The Essential Commentary states: This sutra is a self-proclaimed teaching spoken without being requested.
It is empowered by ultimate great compassion, enabling sentient beings of the Dharma-ending age who face many obstacles to ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression by relying upon it.

Therefore, when the teachings of the future sutras have been extinguished, this sutra alone will remain in the world for a hundred years to extensively deliver all conscious beings. It is like the *agada* medicine that cures all ailments.
It is the dhāraṇī that transcends all dependencies and is perfectly interfused, inconceivable. It is the profound treasury of the Avataṃsaka and the secret marrow of the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka;
it is the essential core of the hearts of all Buddhas and the compass for the myriad practices of Bodhisattvas—all of these do not go beyond this.

The Buddha addressed Ānanda: "In the remote past, incalculable kalpas ago, the Buddha Lokeśvararāja appeared in the world."

World-Honored One, at that time there was a king who, upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, felt great joy in his heart and immediately resolved to attain supreme, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Abandoning his kingdom and renouncing his royal status, he became a śramaṇa named Dharmākara.

He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and stood with palms joined, addressing the Buddha: "World-Honored One, please deign to listen and consider me as I..."
I shall now fully set forth my vows. First Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Second Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should, after the end of their lives, fall again into the three evil paths, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Third Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, within my land...
Fourth Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land do not all possess bodies of true golden color, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Fifth Vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land do not know their past lives—even down to knowing hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas—may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

Regarding the matters of the kalpas: my sixth vow is that if, upon attaining true awakening, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine eye—down to the point of being able to see hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands—I shall not attain true awakening.

My seventh vow is that if, upon attaining true awakening, the devas and humans in my land should not obtain the divine ear—down to the point of being able to hear hundreds of thousands of billions... [of Buddhas].
Eighth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are those among the Buddhas spoken of by nayutas of Buddhas whom I am unable to receive and uphold, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Ninth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land are unable to perceive the minds of others through their own wisdom—even to the extent of knowing the mental activities of sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands—may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Tenth Vow: If I...

May I attain Buddhahood. If the devas and humans in my land are unable to attain the power of spiritual travel (*ṛddhi-pāda*), such that in a single thought-moment they cannot traverse even hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the tenth vow. The eleventh vow:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land should give rise to thoughts of attachment and calculation regarding their own bodies, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the eleventh.
Twelfth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the gods and humans in my land should not abide in the stage of certainty and necessarily reach extinction, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Thirteenth Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, my light should have limits, even failing to illuminate hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands below, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Fourteenth Vow: If, when I attain... [text continues]
The Buddha’s lifespan shall have a finite measure; until it reaches at least one hundred thousand *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas, he will not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the fourteenth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the *śrāvakas* in my land should be able to calculate [the number of my followers], even if all sentient beings in a trichiliocosm were to become *pratyekabuddhas* and together for a hundred thousand kalpas were to collectively compute and know [their number]—[if this were possible, I would not attain enlightenment].

Regarding the number [of vows]: "I shall not attain perfect enlightenment unless, when I become a Buddha, the lifespan of the devas and humans in my land is immeasurable and limitless—except for those who, by their own original vow, have mastery over the length of their lives. If this were not so, I would not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the fifteenth vow.

The sixteenth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be even the sound of the name of anything unwholesome heard among the devas and humans in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The seventeenth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the immeasurable Buddhas of the worlds in the ten directions [should not praise my virtues]...
If those who do not all praise me and call upon my name were not to attain perfect enlightenment—this is the eighteenth vow.

If, when I have attained Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions, with a sincere heart of faith and joy, desire to be born in my land, yet even with as few as ten recitations of my name they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
I shall not attain perfect enlightenment, except for those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the true Dharma. This is the nineteenth vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions who have resolved their minds on Bodhi, cultivated various merits, and with a sincere heart made a vow desiring to be born in my land—
Twentieth Vow: If, upon the time of my death, I do not appear before that person surrounded by a great assembly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Twenty-first Vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, there are sentient beings in the ten directions who hear my name, fix their thoughts upon my land, plant the roots of virtue, and with a sincere heart dedicate their merits toward rebirth in my land, yet fail to achieve their goal, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

The Awakening. The twenty-first vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land do not all fully achieve the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The twenty-second vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of bodhisattvas from other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land do not ultimately reach the stage of being 'one birth short of Buddhahood' (ekajātipratibaddha), with the exception of—"
Transformed by the mastery of his original vows, he donned the armor of the great vow for the sake of sentient beings. Having accumulated the roots of virtue, he delivers all beings;

he travels through the lands of the Buddhas, cultivates the practices of a bodhisattva, makes offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, and transforms immeasurable sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, establishing them in the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, and causing them to transcend the various stages that exceed ordinary measure.
...and practice the conduct of Samantabhadra. If it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The twenty-third vow:

"If, when I become a Buddha, the Bodhisattvas in my land, empowered by the Buddha's spiritual strength, should be unable to travel to countless, immeasurable billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands within the time of a single meal to make offerings to all Buddhas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
I shall attain perfect enlightenment. This is the twenty-fourth vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land, before the presence of all Buddhas, manifest their roots of virtue, yet the various requisites they seek for making offerings do not appear as they wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
This is the twenty-fifth vow. If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land are unable to expound upon all [dharmas]...
If, when I attain Buddhahood, I do not become a Perfectly Enlightened One, I shall not take supreme enlightenment. This is the twenty-sixth vow.
If, when I attain Buddhodyhood, the Bodhisattvas in my land do not obtain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength, I shall not take supreme enlightenment. This is the twenty-seventh vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land, as well as all things therein, are not adorned with pure radiance and exquisite beauty, their forms and colors being uniquely distinguished and reaching the ultimate limit of subtlety, I shall not take supreme enlightenment. This is the twenty-eighth vow.

Exquisite! It is impossible to measure. If there were any sentient beings, even those who have attained the divine eye, who could clearly discern its names and numbers, I would not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the twenty-eighth vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the Bodhisattvas in my land—even those of the least merit—should be unable to know and see the immeasurable radiance and colors of the tree of the Way-Place, rising high..."
If, after forty million *li*, I do not attain perfect enlightenment—this is the twenty-ninth vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land who receive, read, recite, uphold, and explain the Dharma should not obtain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment—this is the thirtieth vow.
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land should...
"If there were any limit to what could be measured, I would not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirty-first vow:

'If, when I attain Buddhahood, my land is so pure that it illuminates and reveals all the infinite, innumerable, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, as clearly as one sees one's own face in a bright mirror—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirtieth [vow]."

The second vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, everything from the ground upward to the void—including palaces, towers, pavilions, ponds, streams, flowering trees, and all the myriad things within my land—were not composed entirely of immeasurable varieties of miscellaneous jewels and hundreds of thousands of kinds of fragrances, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
They shall be joined together to form a single body, exquisitely adorned and wondrous, surpassing all devas and humans.

Its fragrance shall pervade the worlds of the ten directions, and any bodhisattvas who smell it shall all cultivate the practices of a Buddha. If this should not be so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirty-third vow:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the sentient beings of the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions..."
May all beings who encounter my light and whose bodies are touched by it have their bodies and minds become supple and soft, surpassing those of devas and humans.
If this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The thirty-fourth vow:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the various classes of sentient beings in the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should not attain the Bodhisattva stage of non-arising...

The thirty-fifth vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be women in any of the immeasurable and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, [and they do not attain rebirth as men, I shall not take perfect enlightenment]."
Rejoicing with faith and delight, they shall resolve to attain Bodhicitta. If, after the end of their lives, they were again to take on a female form, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

This is the thirty-sixth vow. Furthermore, if I attain Buddhahood, may all the bodhisattvas in the infinite and inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, constantly practice [the path] after the end of their lives.
The Brahma-conduct. Until I attain the Way of Buddhahood—if this be not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The thirty-seventh vow:

Should I attain Buddhahood, if there be gods and humans in the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who, upon hearing my name, prostrate themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, bowing their heads in worship, and with joy, faith, and delight, cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva—[if they do not all attain birth in my land, may I not attain perfect enlightenment].
Devas and humans of the world shall all pay him homage; if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the thirty-eighth vow:

"If, when I attain Buddhahood, the devas and humans in my land who desire clothing should have it appear before them as soon as they think of it—fine garments of wondrous quality, in accordance with the Dharma as praised by the Buddhas—and these should naturally appear upon their bodies, yet there should be those who seek to cut, sew, beat, dye, or wash them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

[The Buddha] said: "The thirty-ninth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the happiness experienced by the devas and humans in my land should not surpass that of the bhikṣus who have exhausted their outflows (āsravakṣaya), may I not attain perfect enlightenment. The fortieth vow:

If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas in my land should wish to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure buddha-lands of the ten directions, may these appear before them at will and according to their aspiration, [manifesting] within the jeweled trees."
All within [the Buddha-field] shall be clearly perceived and seen, just as one beholds the reflection of one’s own face in a bright mirror.
If this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-first vow.

If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any among the assembly of bodhisattvas in other lands who, upon hearing my name, fail to have their various faculties become complete and free from deficiency by the time they attain Buddhahood, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-second vow.
The Forty-second Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, the bodhisattvas of other lands who hear my name do not all attain the Samādhi of Pure Liberation and,

while abiding in this samādhi, fail to worship immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in a single moment of thought without losing their concentration, then may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
I shall attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-third vow:
"If, when I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas from other lands who hear my name should not, at the end of their lives, be born into noble families, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."

The forty-fourth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in lands of other quarters, upon hearing my name, should not experience joyful exultation, cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva, and become fully endowed with the roots of virtue—if this were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The forty-fifth vow: If, when I attain Buddhahood, the multitude of Bodhisattvas in lands of other quarters, upon hearing my [name]...

By name, they shall all attain the Samādhi of Universal Equality. Abiding in this samādhi until they reach Buddhahood, they shall constantly behold immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas of all directions.
If it were not so, I would not take perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-sixth vow.
Furthermore, if I attain Buddhahood, may the bodhisattvas in my land, according to their respective aspirations, hear whatever Dharma they desire to hear from themselves—
Nevertheless, I shall attain sainthood; were it not so, I would not take perfect enlightenment as my realization. The forty-seventh vow:
"If, when I become a Buddha, the multitude of bodhisattvas in other lands who hear my name should not immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
I shall not attain perfect enlightenment. This is the forty-eighth vow:

"If, when I become a Buddha, the bodhisattvas of other lands who hear my name do not immediately attain the first, second, and third stages of dharma-patience, and cannot immediately attain non-retrogression regarding all Buddha-dharmas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. At that time, the Bhikṣu Dharmākara...
Having spoken these vows, at that moment the entire earth shook in six ways, and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers, scattering them over him.
From the sky, a voice proclaimed: "He shall certainly and inevitably attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

The Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (Chapter on the Nine Grades of Visualization), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kuṅ-liang-ye-she of the Western Regions during the Liu Song Dynasty.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "If you wish to give rise to a sincere mind to be reborn in the Western Quarter, you should first practice the visualization of..."

The image one zhang and six chi tall appears upon the waters of the pond. As previously stated, the physical dimensions of Amitāyus Buddha are boundless and are not within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings.
Nevertheless, by virtue of that Tathāgata’s power of past vows, for those who bring him to mind through recollection and contemplation, [he appears].
One will certainly attain accomplishment. Merely by visualizing the Buddha’s image, one gains immeasurable merit; how much more so by contemplating the Buddha’s complete physical marks!
Amitābha Buddha possesses supernormal powers at will; he manifests himself freely throughout the lands of the ten directions.
He may manifest a great body that fills the void of space, or he may manifest a small body of eight feet or six feet in height. All manifested forms are of a true golden color.
The halo manifests transformed Buddhas and precious lotus flowers, as described above.

As for the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in all places their bodies are identical to those of sentient beings; one can only know them to be Avalokiteśvara or Mahāsthāmaprāpta by observing the marks on their heads.
These two Bodhisattvas assist Amitābha Buddha in universally transforming all beings; this is known as "mixed visualization."
Contemplation. This is called the thirteenth contemplation.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Regarding those of the highest grade of the highest birth:

if there are sentient beings who wish to be born in that land and give rise to three kinds of mind, they shall immediately attain birth there. What are these three? First, the mind of utmost sincerity; second..."
These are the mind of deep resolve, the mind of dedication and aspiration, and the mind of practice. One who possesses these three minds will certainly be born in that land.

Furthermore, there are three kinds of sentient beings who shall attain rebirth there. What are the three? First, those who possess a heart of compassion and do not kill, and who fulfill all the precepts and practices.
Second, those who read and recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras. Third, those who cultivate the six mindfulnesses and dedicate their merit toward rebirth.
He makes a vow, praying to be born in that land. Possessing these merits, after one day up to seven days, he shall immediately attain rebirth there.

At the time of his birth in that land, because this person has been diligent and courageous, Amitābha Tathāgata, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, countless transformation Buddhas, hundreds of thousands of bhikṣus, the great assembly of śrāvakas, immeasurable devas, and the seven... [heavenly beings].
The jeweled palace, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva holding a vajra platform, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva will appear before the practitioner.
Amitābha Buddha will emit a great radiance that illuminates the practitioner’s body, and he, along with the various bodhisattvas, will extend his hands to welcome them.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with countless bodhisattvas, will praise the practitioner and encourage their progress.
The practitioner, having seen this, rejoices and leaps for joy. Seeing himself mounted upon a vajra pedestal, following behind the Buddha, he is reborn in that land in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Having been born in that land, he beholds the physical body of the Buddha, complete with all its marks;
he beholds the bodhisattvas, complete with their physical forms; and he sees the jewel groves of radiant light expounding the sublime Dharma. Upon hearing it, he immediately...

They realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). In the space of a mere moment, they serve various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions and receive successive predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) in the presence of those Buddhas.
Returning to their own land, they attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates.
These are called those who are born in the highest grade of the highest level.

Regarding those of the highest grade who are born through middle-level practice: they need not necessarily uphold, read, or recite the Vaipulya sutras. They skillfully understand their meanings and purports;
their minds are not startled or shaken by the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); they have deep faith in cause and effect, and do not slander the Mahāyāna.

By means of these merits, they dedicate them toward the vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. When such practitioners are about to reach the end of their lives, Amitābha Buddha, together with...
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of followers and retinues, holding a purple-golden platform, arrive before the practitioner and praise them, saying:
"O Son of the Dharma, you practice the Mahāyāna and have realized the ultimate truth; for this reason, we have now come to welcome you.
Together with a thousand transformation Buddhas, they simultaneously extend their hands. The practitioner sees themselves seated upon the purple-golden platform and joins their palms.
With palms joined, he praised all the Buddhas. In the space of a single thought-moment, he was reborn within a pool of the seven treasures in that land.

This purple-golden platform was like a great jewel-flower; after one night had passed, it opened. The practitioner’s body was the color of polished purple-gold, and beneath his feet were likewise lotus flowers of the seven treasures.
The Buddha and the Bodhisattvas simultaneously emitted light, illuminating the practitioner’s body, and his eyes immediately—
He became enlightened. Due to his past habitual tendencies, he universally heard all sounds, which exclusively expounded the profound ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
He immediately descended from the golden platform, prostrated to the Buddha with palms joined, and praised the World-Honored One.

After seven days had passed, he attained non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that very moment, he was able to fly, traveling everywhere throughout the ten [directions].
Subsequently, he served various Buddhas and, in the presence of those Buddhas, cultivated various samādhis for the duration of one small kalpa.
He attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and received a prediction of enlightenment in their presence. This is called the person of the highest grade of middle birth.

As for those of the highest grade who are born in the lower station: they also believe in cause and effect and do not slander the Mahāyāna; they simply give rise to the mind set on the unsurpassed path.
By means of these merits, they dedicate them with the vow to seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

When the practitioner’s life is about to end, Amitābha Buddha, along with Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the various bodhisattvas, holding golden lotus flowers, manifest five hundred [transformations].
The Buddha comes to welcome this person. Five hundred manifested Buddhas simultaneously extend their hands and praise them, saying:

"O Son of the Dharma, you have now purely resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment; I come to welcome you. When they see this, they immediately perceive themselves sitting upon a golden lotus flower.
Once seated, the flower closes, and following behind the World-Honored One, they attain rebirth within a pond of the seven treasures in a single day.

The lotus flower opened in a single night, and within seven days, he was able to see the Buddha. Although he saw the Buddha’s body, his mind was not yet clear regarding its various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
After twenty-one days had passed, he saw them with perfect clarity. He heard various sounds, all of which expounded the wondrous Dharma;
he traveled through the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, and before those Buddhas, he heard the most profound teachings. Thus it is said in the sutra.

After three small kalpas, one attains the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas and dwells in the Stage of Joy; this is called "one who is born in the lower grade of the superior class," and this is what is meant by the "conception of being born in the superior class."
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Regarding those of the highest grade among the middle class of rebirth:

if there are sentient beings who uphold the five precepts, observe the eightfold fast, and practice various moral disciplines; who do not commit the five heinous crimes and are free from all faults and afflictions;
and who, by means of these roots of goodness, dedicate their merit with the vow to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss—then at the time of their death, Amitābha..."
The Buddha, surrounded by his retinue of bhikṣus, emitted a golden light and went to that person’s location.
He preached on suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and praised the life of renunciation as the means to escape all sufferings. Upon seeing this, the practitioner felt great joy;
he saw himself sitting upon a lotus pedestal, kneeling with palms joined, prostrating before the Buddha, before even raising his head.
In an instant, they attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The lotus flower opens immediately; as it blooms, they hear various sounds praising the Four Noble Truths.
At that very moment, they attain the path of Arhatship, possessing the three insights, the six supernatural powers, and the eight liberations.
These are called those who are born in the highest grade of the middle class.
Regarding those born in the middle grade of the middle level: if there are sentient beings who, for one day and one night, observe the eight precepts of the fast;
or for one day and one night, observe the śrāmaṇera precepts; or for one day and one night, observe the full set of precepts (upasaṃpadā), with their dignified conduct (īryāpatha) remaining flawless.
By means of these merits, one dedicates them with the vow to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Perfumed by the fragrance of the precepts, when such a practitioner is about to pass away, they will see Amitābha Buddha together with his retinue, emitting golden light and holding a lotus flower made of the seven treasures, appearing before the practitioner.
The practitioner will personally hear a voice in the air praising them, saying: "O son of good family..."
"O virtuous person, because you have followed the teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, I have come to welcome you.
The practitioner will see for himself that he sits upon a lotus flower, which then closes; he is born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

Within a jeweled pond, after seven days have passed, the lotus flower opens. Once the flower has opened, he opens his eyes, joins his palms, and praises the World-Honored One, hearing [the Buddha’s voice]."
Rejoicing in the Dharma, they attain the stage of *srotāpanna*. After half a kalpa has passed, they become *arhats*. These are called those who are born into the middle grade within the middle class.
As for those who are born into the lower grade within the middle class: if there are good men or good women who filially support their parents and practice worldly benevolence...

Maitreya, when this person’s life is about to end, they encounter a spiritual friend who extensively explains for them the joyful matters of Amitābha Buddha’s land and also the forty-eight vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara. Having heard these things, their life immediately comes to an end.
Just as it takes a strong man only the time it takes to bend and extend his arm, they are reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. After seven days have passed—
Having met Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, they hear the Dharma with joy and attain the stage of Srotāpanna. After one minor kalpa has passed, they become Arhats.
These are called those who are born in the lower grade of the middle class; this is termed the perception of birth in the middle grade.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Regarding those of the highest grade of the lower level of rebirth:

there may be sentient beings who have committed various evil deeds, yet do not slander the Vaipulya sūtras. Such foolish people have produced many unwholesome dharmas and lack a sense of shame or remorse.
When their lives are about to end, they encounter a virtuous friend who recites for them the titles of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras."
By hearing the names of such sutras as these, one eliminates the extremely heavy evil karma of a thousand kalpas.
Furthermore, the wise teacher instructs [the practitioner] to join their palms and, with hands clasped, to recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha.

By reciting the Buddha’s name, one eliminates the sins of birth and death for fifty billion kalpas. At that time, that Buddha immediately dispatches transformation Buddhas, transformation Avalokiteśvara, and transformation Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
He arrived and stood before the practitioner, praising him, saying: "O son of good family, because you have invoked the name of the Buddha, all your transgressions have been extinguished;
I have come to welcome you. Having spoken these words, the practitioner immediately saw the light of the manifested Buddha pervading his entire room.
Having seen this, they rejoice and immediately pass away. Riding upon precious lotus flowers, they follow behind the manifested Buddhas and are born within a pool of jewels.
After seven times seven days have passed, the lotus flowers finally bloom.

At the moment the flowers bloom, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion and the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta emit great radiance, stand before those beings, and preach for them the profound twelvefold division of the scriptures.

Having heard this sutra, they believe and understand it, giving rise to the mind set on supreme enlightenment. After ten minor kalpas, they become fully endowed with the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas and attain entry into the first stage (bhūmi).
This is called the "lower grade of the superior birth."

The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī: "As for those born in the middle grade of the lowest level, there may be sentient beings who violate the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the full set of monastic precepts.
Such foolish people steal the property of the Saṃgha as a whole or the property belonging to the resident monks."
They preach the Dharma impurely and lack a sense of shame or remorse. Adorned with various evil karmas, such sinners, by virtue of those evil deeds, ought to fall into hell.
When their lives are about to end, the manifold fires of hell arrive all at once.
Upon encountering a virtuous friend, who out of great compassion immediately extols for them the ten powers and majestic virtue of Amitābha Buddha,
extensively praising that Buddha’s radiant spiritual power, as well as his precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; having heard this,
the person eliminates the offenses of birth and death from eighty billion kalpas, and the fierce fires of hell are transformed into cool clarity.
The wind blows the celestial flowers, and upon each flower are transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who welcome this person.
In the space of a single thought-moment, they attain rebirth within a lotus flower inside a pool of the seven treasures. After six kalpas have passed, the lotus flower finally opens.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with their Brahma-voices, comfort that person and preach for them the Great Vehicle’s profound...

Having heard this profound sutra and this Dharma, they immediately give rise to the aspiration for supreme enlightenment at that very moment; these are called those who attain birth in the middle grade of the lower level.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "As for those who attain birth in the lowest grade of the lower level, there may be sentient beings who have committed unwholesome deeds."

Regarding karma: having committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, and being fully possessed of all manner of unwholesome acts, such a foolish person, by reason of these evil karmas, ought to fall into the evil realms and undergo suffering without end for many kalpas.

Yet, when such a foolish person reaches the moment of death, they encounter a good spiritual friend who provides various forms of consolation, preaches the wondrous Dharma to them, and instructs them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Though that person is oppressed by suffering and has no leisure to mindfully recollect [the Buddha], [they nevertheless do so].
The Buddha said: "Good Friend, if you are unable to keep that Buddha in mind, you should instead invoke the name of Amitāyus Buddha.
In this way, with a sincere heart, let the sound not cease for ten full recitations, calling out: 'Namo Amitābha Buddha.
Because of invoking the Buddha's name, in every thought-moment, the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death will be eliminated. At the time of the end of life, you shall see..."
A golden lotus flower, like a solar disc, will appear before that person. In the space of a single thought-moment, they will attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
Within the lotus, twelve great eons (*mahākalpa*) must pass before the flower finally opens.

Then, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of great compassion, will extensively expound for them the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the methods for extinguishing sinful states. Upon hearing this—
Having rejoiced, they immediately give rise to the bodhicitta at that very moment. This is called one who attains birth in the lower grade of the lowest level;
this is what is meant by the "conception of birth in the lower class.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Those who practice this samādhi shall, in their present bodies, behold the Buddha Amitāyus and the two great [bodhisattvas]."

Good man, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family merely hears the name of the Buddha and the names of these two Bodhisattvas, they shall eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas;

how much more so if they keep them in mind! One who recollects the Buddha should know that this person is a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among men, with Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva as their supreme friends. They shall...
Sitting at the site of enlightenment, one is born into the family of all Buddhas.
When the Great Master Zhiyi was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he commanded that a bed be prepared against the eastern wall, facing westward.

He focused exclusively on reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, had the Forty-eight Vows and the Chapter on the Nine Grades of Contemplation read aloud, and chanted the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Furthermore, [he instructed that...]
Having finished expounding the title of the *Contemplation Sūtra*, he turned to the great assembly, joined his palms in reverence, and praised it, saying: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land;
though there are lotus ponds and jewel trees, few go there. Even those for whom the signs of the fiery chariot have already appeared can still attain rebirth if they repent for a single thought.
How much more so for those who cultivate through precepts and wisdom, whose holy path and power of practice ensure that their merit shall not be in vain."
The Sūtra on the Five Kings and Eight Sufferings Spoken by the Buddha, from the North Canon (Dang-zì-hào), appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin:
In the past, there were five kings whose kingdoms were adjacent to one another. They frequented each other’s realms and did not wage war against one another; they practiced only good.
"Friend, his eldest son is named Prince Puhuan (Universal Peace). He practices the conduct of a bodhisattva, whereas the other four minor princes constantly practice deviant ways.
The Great King feels compassion for them and wishes to deliver them. He summons them to the upper hall to enjoy themselves together for seven days, day and night, performing the music of courtesans.
When the seven days have elapsed, the four minor princes together address the Great King."
He said, "State affairs are many; I request that you return to govern them. The Great King spoke to his attendants, ordering them to prepare the carriages.
The ministers, officials, and commoners all accompanied him as far as the halfway point. At that point, the Great King felt compassion and desired to deliver them [to the truth].
He said to the minor kings, "Each of you speak of the feelings for which you long and find joy. One king replied, "I wish to obtain..."
In the third month of spring, when the trees are in full bloom, to roam and play upon the plains and fields is my joy. Another king spoke again:

"My delight is different; I wish that I might always be a king, with saddled horses and fine attire, surrounded on all sides by towers, pavilions, halls, officials, and subjects—resplendent and dazzling, striking bells and sounding drums as I enter and exit, passing through the streets."
"Fixing my gaze [upon them]—this is my pleasure. Another king spoke again: "My pleasure is different.
I wish to have a fine wife and fine sons, peerless in their beauty, with whom I may enjoy myself and find the utmost delight and satisfaction; this is my pleasure. Another king spoke again:
"My pleasure is yet different. I wish that my parents would always remain, and that I would have many brothers and wives arrayed around me."
They indulge their mouths with fine clothing and delicious food; they find mutual entertainment with plain zithers and simple robes—this is our pleasure.
Having each finished describing what they delighted in, the Four Kings all turned their heads and said to their Great King, "What is it that you delight in?"
The Great King replied: "I shall first speak of what you all delight in, and thereafter speak of my own delight. One of you said:
'In the third month of spring, when the trees are in full bloom, we sport upon the plains; yet in autumn they wither and fall—this is not a lasting joy. Another of you further said:
'May I always be a king, possessing saddled horses, fine attire, and palatial towers and halls.'"
The officials and the people surround him on all sides; brilliant and resplendent, they beat bells and sound drums as he enters and exits, comes and goes, drawing the eyes of passersby.
The former kings, though once majestic and grand, their infinite pleasures having reached their end, find their merit and virtue now utterly exhausted.
When various nations attack one another, they suddenly collapse and perish; this is not long-lasting happiness.

Yet you alone say, "I wish for a fine wife and fine children, peerless in their beauty, with whom I may enjoy myself and indulge my passions to the full. One day, when illness strikes, your grief and suffering will be immeasurable;
this is not long-lasting happiness. You alone further say, "I wish for my parents to remain forever, and that I have many..."
