I take refuge and repent. (Rise to bow, then kneel again and hold the incense burner, saying:)
I prostrate with all my heart and repent: I, disciple [Name], together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, from time immemorial until now...
Enveloped by ignorance and deluded by perversion, they cultivate unwholesome dharmas through the six sense organs and the three karmas,

extensively committing the ten evil deeds, the five acts of immediate retribution, and all manner of transgressions— immeasurable, boundless, and beyond description. Although the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly abide in the world,
their Dharma sounds never cease, wondrous fragrances fill all space, the flavor of the Dharma overflows the void, and they radiate purity.
The radiance illuminates all things; the eternally abiding wondrous principle pervades the void.
Since beginningless time, my six sense faculties have been internally blind and my three karmas have been shrouded in darkness. I have neither seen nor heard, neither awakened nor known.

Due to these causes and conditions, I have long drifted in the cycle of birth and death, traversing the evil realms for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas without any prospect of escape. As the Sūtra says: "Vairocana..."
It pervades all places. The dwelling place of that Buddha is named Constant Tranquil Light.
Therefore, you should know that there are no dharmas whatsoever that are not the Buddha-dharma. Yet, I failed to understand this and followed the flow of ignorance;
thus, within Bodhi I perceived impurity, and within liberation I gave rise to fetters. Now I have finally awakened; now I have finally repented. I come before you to pay homage.
[叩] To all Buddhas and the World-Honored One Amitābha, I openly confess and repent.

May it cause me and all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm—regarding all grave offenses committed by the three karmas and six sense faculties throughout beginningless time, whether currently being committed or yet to be committed; whether performed by oneself, incited in others, or rejoiced in upon seeing or hearing;
whether remembered or not remembered, recognized or not recognized, doubted or not doubted, concealed or revealed—may they all be completely purified.
Ultimately pure. Having completed my repentance, my six sense organs and three karmas are purified and free from blemish or defilement. All roots of goodness I have cultivated are likewise pure.
I dedicate them all to adorn the Pure Land and to ensure that I may be born together with all sentient beings in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
I pray that Amitābha Buddha will constantly come to protect and sustain me, causing my roots of goodness to increase and advance before my eyes, so that I shall never lose this purity.
At the time of death, may my body and mind be endowed with right mindfulness, and my sight and hearing be clear and distinct.
May I behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face, together with the assembly of holy beings, who hold lotus pedestals in their hands to welcome and lead me forth.

In a single kṣaṇa, may I be born before the Buddha, fully possessing the path of a bodhisattva, and extensively deliver all sentient beings so that we together realize the wisdom of all modes (Recite this three times; if time is short or circumstances are urgent, reciting it once is also sufficient). [Then, arise.]
Having completed the repentance and made the vow, take refuge and pay homage to Amitābha Buddha and all the Triple Gem (one prostration).

(Next, perform the circumambulation of the Dharma—either three times, seven times, or many times. Recite [the name] in this manner as you circumambulate according to your inclination; the number of circuits is not restricted. Recite as follows:)
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva.
Homage to the assembly of pure great ocean-like Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind. (Prostrate)
I take refuge in the Dharma. May all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.

(Prostrate. I take refuge in the Sangha. May all sentient beings lead and manage the great assembly, free from all obstacles. (Prostrate. Homage to the Noble Assembly. (Next, proceed to a separate seat.

Recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* or the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. If one is unable to recite the sutra, single-mindedly chant the Buddha’s name for a measured period of time. It is also permissible to perform the dedication of merit and the summary of the practice.)
Regarding the gate of ten recitations (*daśa-smṛty-upasthāna*): every morning, having finished dressing and facing west, stand upright with palms joined.
Recite the name of Amitābha Buddha in a continuous voice; one full breath constitutes one recitation. Ten such breaths constitute ten recitations.

The number of invocations is not limited by the length of the breaths, provided that the breath is used as the measure. The tone should be neither too high nor too low, neither too slow nor too hurried, but kept balanced and even.
When one attains the middle state, the ten breaths are linked together so that the mind does not scatter; to apply oneself with single-minded diligence is what is called "ten recollections.
This means using the breath to bind the mind. Having formed this recollection, one makes a vow and dedicates the merit, saying:
I, [Name], disciple of the Buddha, with single-minded devotion take refuge in Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

May his pure light illuminate me, and may his compassionate vow embrace me. Now, with right mindfulness, I invoke the name of the Tathāgata for ten moments of thought, seeking birth in the Pure Land for the sake of the path to Bodhi.
According to the Buddha’s original vow: "If there are sentient beings who wish to be born in my land..."

If, from the moment of heartfelt faith and joy up to ten recitations, I should fail to attain birth [in that land], may I not realize perfect enlightenment—excepting only those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the True Dharma.
I now recall that since this life began, I have committed no heinous crime nor slandered the Mahāyāna.
May these ten recitations enable me to enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s vows; by riding upon the power of the Buddha’s compassion, may all my transgressions be extinguished and purified.
Through this increase, when one is about to pass away, one knows for oneself that the time has come;

the body is free from the suffering of illness, the mind is without attachment or craving, and the mind is neither inverted nor distracted, as if entering meditative absorption. The Buddha and the assembly of noble ones will personally hold a golden platform and come to welcome me.

In a single moment of thought, one shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; upon the blossoming of the lotus flower, one shall behold the Buddha, immediately hear the Buddha-vehicle, and suddenly realize the Buddha-wisdom.

One shall extensively deliver sentient beings and fulfill the vow for Bodhi. (Having performed this, one should cease; it is not necessary to prostrate. One must continue throughout this life, not allowing even a single day’s neglect.
By simply pledging not to neglect it, one binds one's own mind and shall attain birth in that land.)

Regarding the gate of binding the object of focus: whether attending to public affairs or private sustenance, or when engaged in various worldly tasks, one should never forget the Buddha even in moments of haste, nor lose sight of the Pure Land.
Just as one remains focused on a pressing matter, one may perform all manner of duties while secretly recollecting the previous practice. Mindfulness of the Buddha is likewise;
if mindfulness is lost, one should repeatedly collect and restore it until, over time, it becomes one's natural disposition. Thus, one acts with ease.

Yun Changyi: The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Suppose there are two people; one is single-mindedly intent on remembering, (representing the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings), while the other is single-mindedly intent on forgetting, (representing sentient beings’ mindfulness of the Buddha). These two people may meet and yet not meet, or see and yet not see.
Because the two remember each other and their mutual remembrance is profound, this continues from birth to birth, such that they are as inseparable as a form and its shadow."

Their conditions are contrary and divergent. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish and pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If a child flees and wanders away, though the mother remembers him, what can she do?
But if the child remembers his mother as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall not be separated or far apart.
If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and contemplate the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future; they shall draw near to the Buddha.
Without going far and without relying on expedient means, one naturally attains the opening of the mind. It is like a person who has been smeared with incense; their body carries a fragrance.

In this way, by binding the mind, one spontaneously and constantly wards off all evil thoughts. Even if one intends to commit an evil deed, because one recollects the Buddha, the evil cannot be accomplished.
Even if one follows through with an evil act, at the time of the karma of evil, the mind remains ever-firm, just as the body possesses that fragrance.
One naturally becomes free from foul odors. Furthermore, if one perceives that an evil thought has subtly arisen in the mind, one should immediately recollect the Buddha;
by the power of the Buddha, that evil thought will naturally subside. It is like a person encountering a peril who seeks a powerful ally and is certain to escape.

Moreover, seeing others suffering, one uses the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha to feel compassion for them, wishing that they may be freed from their suffering, as if releasing them from the bonds of prison.
Because of mindfulness of the Buddha, one gives rise to a heart of compassion and vows to be born in the Pure Land, pledging to rescue one another.
Throughout all experiences of every realm, whether wholesome or unwholesome, by recollecting the Buddha with the mind, one forms aspirations through that mental recollection.
Thus, the King of Samantabhadra’s Vows states: "All evil deeds shall not be accomplished; all wholesome karmas shall be fully harmonized."
It is precisely this intention. Thus, by maintaining the continuous mindfulness of the Buddha within the mind, one can accomplish all merits that serve as causes for purification.
Fearing that it would weary the reader, I shall not elaborate further. Truly, this gateway is of the greatest benefit.
Regarding the "Gateways of All Merit," the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* states that when kings or ministers wish to repent for grave offenses, they should practice five matters:

First, rectify the mind so as not to slander the Triple Gem, not obstruct those who leave the household life, and not create obstacles or difficulties for those practicing the Brahma-faring (i.e., do not commit acts of defilement against the fourfold assembly who uphold the precepts).
Second, provide filial support to one’s parents and serve one’s teachers and elders. Third, govern according to the True Dharma.

The state shall not oppress or deceive its people. On the four six-day fast days (*ṣaḍ-ṣaṣṭhī*), it shall issue mandates throughout its borders, within the reach of its power, to prohibit killing (strictly forbidding fishing and hunting) and to admonish against vice and strife.
Regarding the six fast days: on the eighth day of the waxing moon, the messengers of the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*) patrol the world;

on the fourteenth, the princes of the Four Heavenly Kings patrol; and on the fifteenth, the Four Heavenly Kings themselves patrol. During the waning moon, the twenty-third, twenty-ninth, and thirtieth days follow the same pattern. When the Four Heavenly Kings descend in person, all the celestial bodies, constellations, spirits, and deities accompany them at that time. When they encounter those practicing merit through fasting and precepts, the various devas rejoice together.

This immediately bestows salary and extends one’s lifespan, protecting and sustaining meritorious deeds so that they may be accomplished. Fifth, have deep faith in cause and effect and faith in the One True Path, knowing that the Buddha does not perish.
This is largely identical to the three types of merit within the Sixteen Contemplations; however, it is cited here because Samantabhadra specifically addresses kings and ministers.
This is also the primary cause for the pure karma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. If one belongs to the fourfold assembly of the ordained, one should fully possess [these qualities].

Relying on the three types of merit as practice described in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, one should perform at least one of these merits; whether through mental recollection or verbal expression, it must be dedicated with intentional resolve to become a pure cause.
These four dharma-gates are the direct cause for the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha and rebirth in the Pure Land. One must practice them with focused dedication every day;
only then can one expect with certainty to be born in the Pure Land. As the sutra says: "By practicing this samādhi, one will presently behold Amitābha Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas.
If one hears the names of the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas, the births of immeasurable kalpas will be eliminated."
...the sin of death. How much more so for one who recollects [them]. This person is a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among men;
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta shall be their supreme friends. When they sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), they shall be born into the family of all Buddhas.

In this present life, that Buddha shall dispatch countless transformation Buddhas, transformation Avalokiteśvaras and Mahāsthāmaprāptas, as well as twenty-five Bodhisattvas from the Sahā world, day and night.

They shall provide protection. At all times and in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—they shall not allow evil spirits to find an opportunity, nor shall they suffer any calamities.
They will always be venerated by kings, ministers, and all the people.
The merit thus obtained cannot be calculated even in a single thought-moment; it is such that even the eloquence of a Buddha could not fully extol it. With the exception of...
Who among those unworthy people would hear this and not believe and accept it?
(End) In his later years, the Great Master Youxi made the practice of the *Nehan-gyō* (Sūtra on the Buddha’s Final Nirvāṇa) his daily recitation.

At the time of his death, he sat in the full lotus posture and, using his finger, wrote characters in the air, forming the five characters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before passing away. The wondrousness of the Dharma is verified here.
The Treatise on the Ten Doubts Regarding the Pure Land, Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty. First Doubt:
Since all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take great compassion as their primary vocation, they ought only to vow to be born within the triple world. Why is this so?

If one rescues others from the suffering within the five turbidities and the three miserable realms, why would they seek rebirth in a pure land for their own peace, abandoning sentient beings, lacking great compassion, and acting solely for self-benefit, thereby obstructing the path to Bodhi? Answer: There are two kinds of bodhisattvas.

Those who have long practiced the bodhisattva path and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) are truly subject to such censure. However, those who have not yet attained that patience, as well as beginners...

An ordinary person who has merely resolved their mind [on enlightenment] must necessarily never be separated from a Buddha; only when they have perfected the power of patience (*kṣānti*) are they fit to dwell within the triple world (*tridhātu*) to rescue suffering sentient beings amidst an evil age.

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is impossible for an ordinary person bound by all fetters (*sarvabandhana*) to possess a heart of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and yet wish to be born in an evil age to rescue suffering sentient beings.
Why is this? Because in an evil world, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are powerful and...

The power of patience falters as it turns toward sensory objects; bound by sounds and forms, one falls of one's own accord into the three miserable realms. How then could such a person save sentient beings?

Even if they should happen to be born among humans, the Noble Path is difficult to attain. Perhaps, through the cultivation of merit via generosity and precepts, they may become a king or a high minister.

Though possessing wealth and power, even when encountering spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), they refuse to place their trust in them. Greedy, deluded, and negligent, they commit a multitude of transgressions.
Driven by this evil karma, upon entering the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*), they pass through immeasurable kalpas. Emerging from hell, they receive the body of the poor and lowly;
yet if they do not encounter spiritual friends, they fall back into hell. Thus revolving in saṃsāra until this very day—O person!
It is all like this; this is called the "difficult path. Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "One who cannot save oneself when ill can yet save those who are ill.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* provides an analogy: suppose two people each have relatives drowning in water.

One person, driven by urgency, plunges straight into the water to rescue them, but lacking the power of skillful means (*upāya*), both he and his relatives sink. The other person possesses skillful means; he takes a raft...

By boarding it, they all attain liberation. It is the same for bodhisattvas who have newly resolved [to attain enlightenment]: as long as they have not yet attained the power of *kṣānti* (patience/endurance), they cannot save sentient beings.

For this reason, they must remain close to the Buddha; only after attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can they truly save sentient beings, just like those who have obtained a boat.
Furthermore, the treatise says: "An infant cannot be separated from its mother; if separated from the mother, it might fall into a pit or well, or cry out in thirst for milk."
Upon death, the fledgling bird’s wings and feathers are not yet formed; it clings to the tree and its branches, unable to travel far.
Only when its pinions are fully developed can it fly through the air with mastery and without obstruction. Ordinary beings lack such power;

they can only focus their mindfulness on Amitābha Buddha to bring about samādhi. Because this practice has been perfected, at the moment of death they can concentrate their thoughts and attain rebirth, certain and beyond doubt, beholding Amitābha.
The Buddha, having realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), returns to the triple world.
Riding upon the ship of non-arising, he rescues suffering sentient beings and extensively performs Buddha-activities with complete mastery and freedom. Thus, the Treatise says:

"A practitioner who sports in the hells, having attained the patience of non-arising upon being born in that land, returns to the cycle of birth and death to teach and transform those sentient beings suffering in hell. For this reason.
Those who seek birth in the Pure Land should understand its teachings; the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* calls this the "Easy Path. Second Question:
The essence of all phenomena is empty, originally unarisen, and equally quiescent.
To now abandon this and seek that—does this not contradict reason? A sutra says: "First purify your own mind; when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure."
How is this to be reconciled? The answer is twofold: first, a general response; second, a specific response. Regarding the general response:

if it is argued that seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Amitābha constitutes abandoning this world to seek that one, and thus does not accord with principle, then your own insistence on remaining here and not seeking the West constitutes abandoning that [Pure Land] to cling to this [world], which likewise becomes a sickness and does not accord with principle. Furthermore, turning...
Furthermore, one who does not conceive of seeking birth in that [other] realm, nor seeks birth in this realm, has severed the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* states: "If you should have such a thought—that those who set their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* preach the annihilation of all phenomena—do not have such a thought.
Those who have set their minds on *bodhicitta* do not speak of the characteristic of annihilation regarding phenomena. Second, as for the separate answer: as for non-arising...

Regarding "non-extinction": within the conditions for arising, all phenomena combine; they do not maintain their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and even when one seeks the essence of arising, it cannot be found.
When this arising occurs, it comes from nowhere; therefore, it is called "unborn.

When phenomena disperse, they do not maintain their own intrinsic nature, yet one says, "I am dispersing and ceasing. When this dispersal and cessation occur, they go nowhere; therefore, it is called "non-extinguished. It is not...
This means that apart from those things produced by causes and conditions, there exists something else that is neither born nor extinguished.

Furthermore, it is not that one does not seek birth in a pure land; rather, this is called "non-birth. As stated in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty;

they are also designated as provisional names, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. Moreover: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both together, nor without a cause."

Therefore, one knows non-arising. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "Although one knows that the lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates pure lands to teach and transform all classes of beings.
It further says: "In constructing a palace or residence, if it relies upon solid ground, it can be completed as desired without hindrance;
if it relies upon empty space, it can never be accomplished. The Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma always relies upon the two truths and does not destroy them."
Using provisional names, one speaks of the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. The wise person ardently seeks birth in the Pure Land, yet realizes that the essence of birth is unattainable;
this is precisely non-arising. This is what is meant by "when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. The ignorant, however, are bound by birth.
Upon hearing of "arising," one immediately forms the conceptualization of arising; upon hearing of "non-arising," one immediately forms the conceptualization of non-arising.

Not knowing that arising is itself non-arising and that non-arising is itself arising, they fail to penetrate this principle and recklessly engage in disputes over right and wrong, resenting others for seeking birth in the Pure Land—how much slanderous this is!
Such people are slanders of the Dharma; they are heterodox practitioners of false views.
The third doubt: The pure lands of all ten directions are equal in their *dharmatā*, and their merits are likewise equal.
A practitioner should universally recollect all these merits in order to be born in all pure lands; yet, now you seek only the pure land of a single Buddha, which contradicts the nature of equality.

Answer: The lands of all Buddhas are indeed equal. However, because the faculties of sentient beings are dull and they are mired in turbidity and confusion, [they are directed toward a specific land].
If one's mind is not fixed on a single object, samādhi is difficult to achieve. To focus one’s mindfulness exclusively on Amitābha Buddha is precisely the *ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi* (one-mark samādhi).
By means of such single-minded devotion, one attains rebirth in that land. This is according to the *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows*, wherein the Bodhisattva Puguang asks:
"There are pure lands in all ten directions. For what reason do you praise only the western direction? The Buddha told Puguang:

"The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa have minds that are mostly turbid and distracted. By praising the pure land of a single Buddha exclusively, they are enabled to focus their minds on a single object, whereby they may attain rebirth there."
If one contemplates all Buddhas collectively, the object of focus is so vast that the mind becomes distracted, making it difficult to achieve samādhi; therefore, [the state] cannot arise.
Furthermore, seeking the merit of a single Buddha is no different from seeking the merit of all Buddhas, because they share the same Buddha-nature (*dharmatā*).
For this reason, to contemplate Amitābha Buddha is to contemplate all Buddhas; to be born in one pure land is to be born in all.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The bodies of all Buddhas are the body of a single Buddha. Their single mind and single wisdom, as well as their powers and fearlessnesses, are likewise so.
It further says: "Just as the pure full moon universally appears in all waters, though its reflections are infinite, the original moon has never been two.
In this same way, with unimpeded wisdom, one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment and manifests accordingly."
In all lands, the Buddha-body is non-dual. The wise understand this through analogy:
they are able to realize that all moon-reflections are the reflection of a single moon, and the reflection of a single moon is all moon-reflections, because the substance of the moon is non-dual.
Thus, one Buddha is all Buddhas, and all Buddhas are one Buddha, because the Dharma-body is non-dual. Therefore, ardently recollect one Buddha.
"Time" refers to the mindfulness of all Buddhas. Regarding the fourth inquiry:
"If one can attain rebirth by mindfully recollecting any single Buddha-land among the lands of the ten directions, why focus specifically on Amitābha Buddha?
The answer is: ordinary beings lack wisdom and do not dare to act independently; they must rely exclusively on the words of the Buddha, as taught throughout Śākyamuni’s entire lifetime of preaching.

Throughout the various sections of the sublime teachings of the Dharma, there is only the exhortation for sentient beings to mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and seek rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
This is because more than several dozen texts, such as the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, the *Contemplation Sūtra*, and the *Treatise on Rebirth*, diligently provide these instructions;
therefore, one should focus exclusively on this mindfulness. Furthermore, Amitābha possesses a distinct set of forty-eight great compassionate vows to receive and guide sentient beings. Moreover—
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that Amitābha Buddha possesses eighty-four thousand primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Each mark has eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).

Each secondary sign emits eighty-four thousand rays of light, which pervasively illuminate the Dharma-realm and sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, gathering them in and never abandoning them.
If there are those who practice such mindfulness, when their capacity and the response coincide, they will certainly attain rebirth. Furthermore, the *Amitābha Sūtra*...
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra of King Drum-Sound*, and others state that when Śākyamuni Buddha preached these sūtras,

all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extended their tongues to cover the great trichiliocosm, thereby certifying that all sentient beings who mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha will,
by virtue of the power of the Buddha’s great compassion and original vow, certainly attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Regarding the Land of Bliss, one should know that Amitābha Buddha has a particularly close affinity with this world.

At the time when the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* is about to perish, he specifically causes this sūtra to remain in the world for another hundred years to guide sentient beings toward rebirth in his land;
thus, we know that Amitābha Buddha has a particularly close affinity with the most wicked sentient beings of this world.
Although other pure lands are briefly encouraged in one or two sutras, they do not match the diligent exhortations found throughout the sutras and treatises regarding the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Fifth question: An ordinary person bound by all fetters possesses heavy and thick evil karma; not even a hair’s breadth of any affliction has been severed.
The Pure Land of the West transcends the three realms (*tridhātu*). How can those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) attain birth there?

Answer: There are two kinds of conditions: first, self-power (*svabalika*); second, other-power (*parabalika*). Regarding self-power: although one practices the path in this world, in reality, one has not yet attained birth in the Pure Land.

This is precisely the mind that aspires to become a Buddha; the mind that aspires to Buddhahood is the mind that delivers sentient beings;
the mind that delivers sentient beings is the mind that gathers sentient beings into the Buddha-land. Furthermore, to aspire to be born in the Pure Land, one must possess two practices:
first, one must distance oneself from the three kinds of dharmas that obstruct the gate to Bodhi; second, one must attain the three kinds of dharmas that accord with the gate to Bodhi. What are they?

One remains far removed from the three obstacles to the dharma of enlightenment: first, by relying on the gate of wisdom, one does not seek personal happiness, thereby remaining far removed from the egoistic mind that clings to one's own self;
second, by relying on the gate of compassion, one extracts the suffering of all sentient beings, thereby remaining far removed from the mind that finds no peace in the state of sentient beings;
third, by relying on the gate of skillful means, one feels pity for all sentient beings and desires to bestow happiness upon them.

Because one distances oneself from the mind that seeks honor and offerings for its own sake, if one can distance oneself from the three obstacles to bodhi, one will attain the three factors conducive to bodhi.
First is the undefiled, pure mind; because one does not seek various pleasures for one's own sake, bodhi is the state of being undefiled and pure.
If one seeks pleasure for one's own sake, this is an obstacle that defiles the body and mind.
The gate of bodhi; therefore, the unstained and pure mind is the gate that accords with bodhi. Second, the peaceful and pure mind:
because it aims to uproot the suffering of sentient beings, bodhi is the pure state where all sentient beings find peace and security.

If one does not apply the mind to uprooting all sentient beings so as to free them from the suffering of birth and death, one violates the gate of bodhi; therefore, it is the peaceful and pure [mind].
The mind is that which accords with the gateway to Bodhi. It is the pure mind of the threefold bliss, because it desires to cause all sentient beings to attain Great Bodhi and Nirvana.

Since Bodhi and Nirvana are the ultimate abodes of eternal bliss, if one does not resolve to cause all sentient beings to attain this ultimate eternal bliss, one obstructs the gateway to Bodhi. From what cause, then, could this Bodhi be attained?

The essential cause for birth in the Pure Land is to never be separated from the Buddha. Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one rescues suffering sentient beings within the realm of birth and death.

With compassion and wisdom internally integrated, and concentration constantly in operation, one is sovereign and unimpeded; this is precisely the bodhicitta. This is the meaning of the aspiration for birth.
Second, regarding the clarification of the joyful mind that seeks [birth]: one arouses thoughts with a yearning heart, taking Amitābha Buddha as the object of focus.
Whether it be the Dharma-body or the Reward-body, its golden radiance consists of eighty-four thousand marks, each mark possessing eighty-four thousand secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*),
and each secondary sign emitting eighty-four thousand rays of light that constantly illuminate the Dharma-realm,

gathering in those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Furthermore, one contemplates the wondrous bliss and adornments of the seven treasures of that land, as fully described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

The sutras, such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* and the *Sixteen Contemplations*, teach that one should constantly practice the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha, as well as all virtuous deeds such as giving, precepts, and cultivation, dedicating them all to all sentient beings so that they may be born together in that land. One will certainly attain birth there;
this is the gate of joyful aspiration.

Yang Jie said: "The writings that praise and assist the teachings and contemplations of Amitābha are as numerous as mountains; yet, among them, the *Ten Doubts* (Shiyi lun) by Zhiyi stands preeminent.

By citing the words of the Sages, it resolves the doubts of the multitude. It is like the sun suddenly shedding its abundant light into a dark chamber of ten thousand years, or like a boat equipped for a journey of a thousand li, requiring no personal exertion.
This could not have been achieved by anyone other than the reincarnation of Nāgārjuna."
Master Shandao exclusively practiced this Dharma gate.
Upon seeing Master Chao of Xihé’s Pure Land Nine Grades Practice Hall, he said with joy:
"This is truly the essential ford for entering the Buddha-way. Cultivating other practices is circuitous and difficult to accomplish; only this Dharma gate allows for swift transcendence to rebirth."
He died. Thereupon, he applied himself with diligent and earnest austerity, chanting and reciting day and night. Eventually arriving at the capital, he inspired the fourfold assembly;

whenever he entered his room, he would kneel for a long time chanting the Buddha’s name, never ceasing until his strength was exhausted. When he went out, he expounded the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land for over thirty years without ever sleeping.
He upheld the precepts, not violating even the slightest detail. He preferred to provide food for the assembly, even if it were coarse.

He lived frugally for himself. All his offerings and donations were used to transcribe more than one hundred thousand scrolls of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, to paint three hundred wall murals depicting the transformations of the Pure Land, to construct pagodas and temples, and to light lamps to maintain perpetual illumination. Among the monastics and laypeople who followed his teachings, there were many;
some recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* one hundred thousand to five hundred thousand times, while others daily recited the names of the Buddhas.
Among those numbering from ten thousand to one hundred thousand, there were those who attained samādhi and were born in the Pure Land; their number was beyond reckoning.
Someone asked, "Is it by reciting the Buddha’s name that one is born in the Pure Land? Daoyou replied, "It shall be according to what you recite, and thus your vow shall be fulfilled.
He then recited the name once himself, and a ray of light issued from his mouth; when he recited it ten times up to a hundred times, the light did likewise. He then exhorted [the others].
A verse from the world says: Gradually the skin becomes like that of a rooster and the hair turns white like a crane; watch as the gait grows increasingly faltering.
Even if gold and jade fill the hall, how can one avoid decay, aging, and the suffering of illness? No matter how many kinds of pleasures you may have, impermanence will inevitably arrive.
There is only the path of direct cultivation: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Question: For what reason does one not instruct people to practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), but instead directs them solely to recite the Name?

Answer: Sentient beings have heavy afflictions and hindrances; their objects of focus are subtle while their minds are coarse. Their consciousnesses are fluttering and their spirits are scattered, making contemplation difficult to accomplish. Therefore, out of great compassion, the Great Sage directly exhorts them to single-mindedly recite the Name.
This is precisely because the act of reciting the Name is easy, and through it, continuity is immediately established. If one can maintain this from thought to thought...
If ten people continue this until the appointed time, ten will surely be born [in the Pure Land]; if a hundred do so, a hundred will surely be born. Why is this?

Because they are free from external distracting conditions and attain right mindfulness; because they correspond with the Buddha’s original vow; because they do not contravene the teachings; and because they follow the Buddha’s words.
If one abandons single-minded recollection to practice miscellaneous deeds, then among a hundred, perhaps only one or two may succeed; among a thousand, perhaps only three or four.
Why is this? Because they are distracted by various conditions and lose right mindfulness; because it does not accord with the original vows of the Buddha;

because it contradicts the teachings; because it does not conform to the Buddha’s words; because their focused recollection lacks continuity; because their minds do not continue in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness;
and because although they perform deeds and practices, they are constantly associated with fame and profit, delighting in approaching various conditions and thereby obstructing themselves.

Because this obstructs the correct practice for others’ rebirth [in the Pure Land], I have recently observed that among the clergy and laity in various regions, their understanding and practice differ, and their single-mindedness or distraction vary.
If one practices with exclusive devotion, ten out of ten will be reborn there; however, among those who cultivate a mixture of practices without sincerity, not even one in a thousand will succeed.
I pray that all people will reflect well upon this for themselves: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you must strenuously exert your mind and subdue yourself.
Do not let this cease by day or night; let the end of your life be the limit for your practice. At the moment the preceding thought ends, the succeeding thought is immediately reborn.
For long durations and eternal kalpas, you shall enjoy the bliss of unconditioned dharmas until you attain Buddhahood. How joyful this is!
When an ordinary person approaches the end of their life and wishes to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, they must first prepare themselves and not fear death.
They should constantly reflect that this body is fraught with manifold sufferings and is entangled by various impure and evil karmas.
If one can cast off this defiled body and transcend to be born in the Pure Land, one will experience immeasurable bliss, behold the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and be liberated from suffering.
This is indeed a matter that accords with one's wishes. It is like casting off foul and tattered garments to exchange them for precious, noble robes.
Relinquish body and mind; do not give rise to craving or attachment. As soon as illness arises—regardless of its severity—one should contemplate impermanence and wait single-mindedly for death.
One must instruct family members and those who come to inquire after one’s health: whenever anyone comes before me, simply recite the Buddha’s name for my sake. Do not...
One may speak of idle and miscellaneous matters before one’s eyes, as well as the long and shortcomings within the family;
however, there is no need for soft words of consolation or prayers for peace and happiness, for these are all empty, flowery, and useless words.

If the illness is grave and death is imminent, relatives must not shed tears or wail, nor raise sounds of lamentation and distress, which would disturb the mind and spirit and cause it to lose its [composure].
Maintain right mindfulness; simply recite the Buddha’s name with one voice at all times to assist in your rebirth there.

It would be a great fortune indeed if those who clearly understand the Pure Land were to come frequently to encourage you. If you rely upon this practice, you will certainly attain rebirth without any doubt.
I have often observed people of this world who, during their ordinary lives, recite the Buddha’s name and make vows to seek rebirth in the Pure Land with great earnestness.
Yet, when they approach the point of death, they again fear dying and say nothing at all about rebirth. This matter of death is of the utmost gravity;

one must exert effort for oneself from the start. If there is even a single moment of error, one will suffer through kalpas of time—no one can take one's place in its stead. Reflect upon this, reflect upon it!
Master Fazhao experienced a vision of Mañjuśrī.
Accompanied by several like-minded companions, he traveled far to Mount Wutai and arrived at Foguang Temple. There, he saw a wondrous light illuminating his body from afar;
he immediately proceeded another fifty li and encountered two youths who called themselves Sudhana and Nanda, and led him [onward].
He arrived at a temple with a sign that read: "The Great Sage Zhulin Temple. Its grounds were adorned with golden soil and precious trees.

Entering the temple, he ascended the lecture hall and saw Mañjuśrī to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, each occupying a lion throne and preaching the Dharma while surrounded by a multitude of ten thousand people.
Huizhao prostrated himself and asked: "In this age of the Final Dharma, ordinary beings are far removed from the time of the Sages. As for spiritual teachers..."
Narrow and inferior, with obstructions and defilements particularly deep, there is no way for the Buddha-nature to manifest. The Buddha-dharma is vast and profound;
I do not yet know which dharma-gate to practice as being most essential. Mañjuśrī replied: "If you now practice mindfulness of the Buddha, this is precisely the right time.
Among all gates of cultivation, none surpasses mindfulness of the Buddha. To make offerings to the Triple Gem is to cultivate both merit and wisdom together. These two gates are the most..."

This is the essential path. Why is this so? Because in past kalpas, it was by virtue of contemplating the Buddha, by virtue of recollecting the Buddha, and by virtue of making offerings to him that I attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Therefore, all dharmas—from the profound meditative concentrations of the *prajñāpāramitā* up to the Buddhas themselves—are born from the recollection of the Buddha. Thus, one should know that all dharmas arise from the recollection of the Buddha.
The King asked, "How should one practice recollection? Mañjuśrī replied, "To the west of this world is Amitābha Buddha.
The power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable; you should maintain recollection continuously and without interruption.

At the end of your life, you will certainly attain rebirth there and never fall back. Having spoken these words, the two great sages extended their golden arms together and rubbed the crown of the King’s head, saying:
Because you have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, you will before long realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
If sons or daughters of good family wish to swiftly attain Buddhahood, there is nothing superior to mindfulness of the Buddha; by doing so, they can quickly realize unexcelled bodhi.
The Dharma Master Huiri experienced a vision of Avalokiteśvara.
The Dharma Master Huiri traveled to the Western Regions in search of the Dharma; after drifting at sea for three years, he successfully reached India.

He paid homage at the sacred sites of the Tathāgata and sought out Sanskrit manuscripts. Having endured many hardships during his travels, he grew weary of Jambudvīpa and longed for some other land or region where there was joy and no suffering.
He asked the Tripiṭaka masters throughout India what dharma or practice could lead one to quickly behold the Buddha, and they all urged him to cultivate the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
Having heard this, Wuzhuo received it upon the crown of his head; gradually, he arrived at Kanyakubja in North India.
In the kingdom of Dhara, there is a great mountain to the northeast of the royal city. Upon this mountain is an image of Avalokiteśvara.

To those who pray with utmost sincerity, the Great Being frequently manifests his form. One person went to the mountain and prostrated himself for seven days, further abstaining from food, vowing to remain until the end of his life.
On the night of the seventh day, Avalokiteśvara appeared in the air with a body of purple-gold, over ten feet in height, seated—
From within the precious lotus flower, he extended his right hand and stroked the crown of the Sun’s head, saying:
"If you wish to transmit the Dharma for the benefit of both yourself and others, you should single-mindedly contemplate Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

Once you have made the vow to be reborn there and have arrived in that land, you shall behold the Buddha and me, thereby attaining great benefit. You must know that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land surpasses all other practices."
The Dharma Master Feixi asked:

"In the Vaipulya sutras, it is taught that one should cultivate supreme and profound meditative concentration (samādhi) by maintaining continuous mindfulness of the white tuft [between the Buddha's brows], while simultaneously reciting the Buddha’s name to pray for this superior concentration.

However, when silent recitation is as clear as a spring, samādhi arrives of its own accord. Why then must there be such clamor in the streets and alleys, with sounds echoing through the neighborhood?"
"Only after shaking the mountains and forests does one attain the Way? He replied, "The sound is indeed not in error. Now, the essence of dispersing obstructions lies in the sound.
If the sound is not stern, the mind will secretly lack stability; there are five meanings to this.

First, like pulling up the thatch grass by its roots, when one follows the whip-stroke, their life’s mission is fulfilled in a single encounter, and they bid long farewell to a hundred anxieties. Second, wherever the radiance of the sound reaches, ten thousand calamities melt away like ice."
II. A forest of merit where the pines flourish across a thousand peaks. III. The golden countenance radiates brilliant splendor, and jeweled flowers drip and rain through the void;
all these are as clear as pointing at one's own palm, for they are conveyed by sound. IV.

Like pulling wood or stone that is heavy and does not move forward, yet when the great sound issues forth its proclamation, it is lifted up lightly and floats away. V. In battle with the demonic armies, their banners and drums face one another.

Fifth, he applied the principles of prosody to his military chariots to ensure victory over powerful enemies. Sixth, by harmonizing both the noisy and the tranquil, and by practicing cessation and contemplation in tandem, he accorded with the intent of the Buddha—is this not most appropriate?
As the *Preface to the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha* states: "The merit is so great that progress is easily made."
Buddha-recitation is the foremost practice. Indeed, when the profound resonance strikes, the dust of accumulated afflictions is always dissolved and obstructed emotions are clarified and brightened.
Were it not for the ultimate subtlety of this world, who could participate in this? Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:

"One would rather undergo immeasurable suffering to hear the Buddha’s voice than receive every kind of pleasure without hearing the Buddha’s name. Thus, the Buddha’s voice resounds afar, opening the way to goodness.
The sprouting [of the seed] is like the spring thunder stirring the hundred grasses. How could one lightly misrepresent this? He asked again:

"Regarding rebirth in the Pure Land through a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*) or ten thought-moments (*daśacitta*), which is the correct teaching? He replied: "Rebirth through a single thought-moment leads to abiding on the stage of non-retrogression;

this is the correct teaching. It is as the Buddha said: slandering the Buddha, destroying the sutras, striking monks, reviling the honored ones, and committing the five heinous crimes or the four grave offenses—all these are evils of a single thought-moment."

When karma is completed, one falls into the Avīci Hell as swiftly as an arrow shot. Now, by recollecting the Buddha and being born in the Pure Land, a single thought of wholesome karma is likewise completed.
One ascends to the Land of Ultimate Bliss as quickly as bending and extending the arm. In the preceding thought, the five aggregates cease; in the succeeding thought, the five aggregates arise.
It is like a wax seal pressed into clay: once the seal is broken, the impression is formed; no second thought is required.

The novice monk who craved curd gave rise to a single thought of craving and was subsequently reborn as an insect within that curd. The wife of the great householder Mahāśāla sat before a bright mirror, gazing at her own body with self-attachment, when a sea wind wrecked her ship and she was reborn as an insect within a decaying corpse.
All of these resulted from a single thought. This is the power of the Great Immeasurable [Life].
The *Amitāyus Sūtra* clarifies that reciting the Buddha’s name even for a single thought-moment ensures rebirth in the Pure Land.

The ten recitations in the *Contemplation Sūtra* were established because those who are afflicted by illness, frail, weak in strength, and inferior in mental power require ten invocations to assist their single thought-moment. If the mind is vigorous and undeluded, rebirth occurs in a single thought-moment.
This is like planting a strand of silk hair; though tiny, it will grow to a girth of a hundred spans.
Chan Master Yongming Shou cautioned against disparaging the Pure Land, saying: Question:
"If one merely perceives one's nature and awakens to the Way, one transcends birth and death. Why then is it necessary to fix the mind on that Buddha and seek rebirth in another land?
Answer: "A true practitioner should examine themselves. It is like a person drinking water: whether it is cold or warm, they know for themselves. [The Master] continued: "Now, let us consider..."
This serves as a mirror for all you virtuous ones to shatter many delusions. You should examine your own conduct and understanding: have you seen your nature and awakened to the Way?

Have you received the prediction of the Tathāgata and succeeded to the rank of the Patriarchs? Can you be like Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna? Have you attained unimpeded eloquence and realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*?
Can you be like the Tiantai Master Zhiyi? Are you proficient in both the doctrine and its exposition, and do you cultivate both practice and understanding? Can you...
Is this not like the case of National Teacher Zhong? These great beings have all clearly bestowed their verbal teachings, deeply exhorting [us] toward rebirth in the Pure Land.

This is surely for the sake of benefiting both oneself and others; how could they ever intend to mislead others or deceive themselves? Moreover, the Great Hero (the Buddha) praised this with his golden mouth and exhorted it with earnest urgency.

We should follow the examples of the sages of old and reverently receive the Buddha’s command; it is certainly not erroneous. As recorded in the *Biographies of Those Who Attained Rebirth*, throughout past and present...
The deeds of the eminent worthies are numerous and manifest; you should diligently study them to reflect upon and understand yourself.

Furthermore, you must examine for yourself whether, at the moment of death, you will attain mastery over the transition between birth and death, or whether you will remain in this world. Will your heavy karmic obstructions from beginningless time certainly not manifest before you?
Will this retribution-body certainly escape the cycle of saṃsāra? And as for the three miserable realms and the various classes of beings in the evil paths—will you be free from them?
Moving through the middle way, appearing and disappearing with freedom—will you certainly be free from suffering and affliction?

Whether in the heavens or among humans, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, will you be able to entrust yourself wherever you wish without any hindrance? If you can attain clear and confident realization of this, what could be more excellent?
If you have not yet reached it, do not be arrogant for a moment, lest you cause yourself to sink into eternal samsara and lose the benefit of the Dharma.
Whom else shall we blame? Alas, how tragic! What lamentation can avail now? **The Fourfold Discernment:** 1.
"If one has Chan but no Pure Land, nine out of ten will go astray. When the realm of the *ālaya* manifests before them, they will instantly follow it away. 2.
"If one has no Chan but has the Pure Land, ten thousand who practice, ten thousand will go. Once you have seen Amitābha, why worry that you will not attain enlightenment?"
The third says: "To have both Chan and the Pure Land is like a tiger with horns; in this life one becomes a teacher of men, and in future lives one becomes a Buddha or a Patriarch.
The fourth says: "Without Chan and without the Pure Land, there are only iron beds and copper pillars; for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there will be no one to rely upon."
The Memorial by the Venerable Master Siming Exhorting the Practice of Buddha-Recitation:
Originally, a single thought is fundamentally harmonious, and all phenomena are without obstruction. Yet, as the conditions of karmic perfuming differ, the resulting retributions vary accordingly.

Therefore, if one practices in accordance with their true nature, the pure lands of the Buddhas are revealed; if one acts according to deluded emotions, one follows the cycle of suffering within the five destinies.

Therefore, for those dwelling in the Sahā world, it is especially difficult to ascend and emerge; those who fall back are numerous. As the Sūtra says: "Those who obtain a human body are like the soil on one's fingernails;
those who lose a human body are like the soil of the great earth. Only when the practices of the Three Vehicles are fully prepared can one avoid rebirth in the four realms of existence.
This is because the objective environment is coarse and powerful, and afflictions are fiercely blazing; to seek liberation through one's own efforts is truly difficult.

As for those who are born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*): the land is adorned with splendor, their bodies and minds are pure, and they proceed directly to the attainment of Buddhahood without falling into the three miserable realms (*apāya*).
As the sutra says: "There is not even the name of the evil paths, let alone their actual existence. It further states: "All sentient beings who are born there are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
If one wishes to be born there, one need only recite the name of that Buddha and cultivate the practice of that Buddha.
O Compassionate One, they shall surely be gathered by the original vows of that Buddha; casting off this reward-body, they will certainly be born in that land.
This is exactly as taught in the sutras and is not a mere speculative discourse. Now, ten thousand people have formed a single society, binding their hearts together in mindfulness.

They have made a solemn vow for every day, and each year during the second month of spring, they gather in one place to collectively perform offerings and listen to the sound of the Dharma. Thus, these ten thousand...
Set your mind with single-minded resolve to accomplish pure karma and vow to attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Furthermore, in this age of defilement, the light of life is like a candle in the wind;
if but one breath fails to reach its end, the three miserable realms will appear before you. How can you afford to be complacent? Do not consider future retributions;
you must rely on the Buddha’s words rather than conforming to human sentiments. Cease all攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to external objects) immediately and strive only in the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
A Verse for Encouraging People to Make Vows by the Patriarch Cizhao:
All phenomena arise from the mind; all phenomena cease within the mind. Our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, has always spoken thus:

If one upholds the precepts but lacks faith and vows, One cannot be born in the Pure Land; One will only obtain the blessings of humans and devas, And when those blessings are exhausted, undergo saṃsāra.

One revolves in saṃsāra, unable to escape. Lacking the eye of wisdom when reading the sutras, one does not understand the Buddha’s profound intent. In future lives, though one may attain intelligence, the distracted mind makes liberation difficult.
By the power of making vows and upholding the precepts, dedicate [merit] toward rebirth in a land of bliss. Thus, each should practice accordingly.
"Among a thousand, not one shall fail. Thus spoke Śākyamuni with his golden mouth. Amitābha personally embraces them; all Buddhas protect and mind them.
All devas skillfully guard and sustain them. Seeing these practitioners of nianfo, they are not far from the Buddha. They should sit at the site of enlightenment."
He turns the Great Dharma Wheel and universally delivers boundless multitudes. It is like the daughter of a poor family who conceives a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) in her womb;
though the gods constantly protect her, the poor woman herself does not know that there is a noble child within her belly. So it is with this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha.
Their intention is likewise thus: they recollect the Buddha and constantly keep him in mind, thinking, "Before long I shall attain Buddhahood.

Though the Buddhas skillfully protect and sustain them, these people do not realize it themselves; they think, "I shall be born in the Pure Land, and later, in a future life, I will again be born among humans."
For example, suppose there were a hidden treasure beneath the ground in the house of a poor man, which a treasure-guarding spirit constantly protects so that it does not go missing.
Yet the poor man himself is unaware that there is a precious treasure within his own home; day after day he seeks work as a laborer, striving to provide for himself with food and clothing.
Now, the intention of this person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha is likewise.

This person who practices mindfulness of the Buddha possesses the Tathāgatagarbha in its entirety, yet they say of themselves, "I have no share in it," and instead seek rebirth among human beings. It is like a sick person's house that possesses a truly wondrous medicine within.
Not knowing the nature of the wondrous medicine, one cannot cure one's own illness; day after day by one's bedside, one suffers immeasurable pain.
Now, it is the same with this person who recites the Buddha’s name: not knowing that the mind of reciting the Buddha can extinguish greed, anger, and delusion.
They can act as great kings of physicians; they can act as great treasuries of jewels, benefiting and aiding all people; they can act as great Dharma-kings, providing protection for all beings.
Yet, if one considers oneself an ordinary person and believes one cannot be born in the Pure Land, one should instead personally observe the fasts and precepts.
In future lives, one vows to become human; through successive rounds of further practice, one may finally be born in that land. Many who see practitioners constantly make such claims:
they do not accord with Amitābha’s vows, nor do they conform to the Pure Land sutras. Their minds are shrouded by the obstruction of false views.
It will be ultimately difficult to escape; it is not the obstacle of another, but entirely the obstacle of one's own mind.
If you do not attain birth in this life, one missed opportunity becomes a hundred. I exhort you, O practitioner: believe the words of the Tathāgata.

The Buddha never speaks anything untrue; how could these be empty or deceptive words? You should simply be diligent for yourself, seeking the Pure Land with a single mind. It is like using wind to fan a fire.
The effort required is not great; fortunately, you possess the mind of *nien-fo*. Dedicate this vow to transcend the three realms.

To encounter a treasure and fail to take it, or to meet with food and suffer long hunger—alas for such a great man! You do not perceive the true meaning. I now offer this brief exhortation and praise.
Pass it on from person to person; for generations, spread it widely. Acting as the Tathāgata’s messenger, you are truly the children of all Buddhas.
This is truly called repaying the Buddha’s kindness. May all practice according to these teachings and together be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

In the *Lianzong baojian* (Jewel Mirror of the Lotus School) by Master Youtan, it is stated that those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name and wish to be reborn in the Pure Land must constantly contemplate that all things in this world are impermanent;

that what is formed must inevitably decay, and that birth must inevitably end in death. If one has not personally heard the Buddha-dharma, then as one discards this body and receives another, one will continue to revolve through the three realms of existence.
Within the realms of the four modes of birth and the six paths of existence, there is no prospect of liberation.

Now that I have the karmic affinity to hear the True Dharma and cultivate pure deeds, I shall take only the Buddha as my object of mindfulness. Upon casting off this retribution-body, I shall be reborn in the Pure Land;
entering the womb of a lotus flower, I shall experience all manner of bliss, forever escape birth and death, and never retreat from Bodhi. This is the lifelong accomplishment of a great man.
As soon as illness occurs, you must immediately strive to broaden and clarify your body and mind; do not give rise to doubt or hesitation.

You must sit facing west in the correct posture, single-mindedly visualizing Amitābha Buddha, along with the Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and countless transformation Buddhas, all appearing before you.
With one-pointed concentration, recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha," ensuring that each sound follows the next without interruption.
Regarding all worldly affairs, one must not harbor thoughts of them nor feel any attachment.
Should such thoughts arise, one must immediately recite the Buddha’s name; in every moment of mindfulness, this will eliminate karmic obstructions.
If the patient is delirious or exhausted and unable to act spontaneously, the caregiver should employ skillful means to rouse and exhort them, advising them in this manner.
Apply your mind with resolve to assist in bringing this life to its end. With this single thought, rebirth in the Pure Land is certain.
If your life has not yet ended, you will naturally attain peace and security. Be careful not to give rise to thoughts of attachment to the world.

You must live when it is time to live, and you must die when it is time to die. Simply prepare for rebirth; why harbor doubts? If you understand this principle, it is like casting off worn-out clothes to put on new ones.
Upper garment. In a single renunciation of the ordinary body, one immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood. How marvelous! How magnificent! It is ultimate; it is exhaustive.
For those who truly believe and practice, it is certain that they must be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
With single-minded focus on a single thought, hold the name of Amitābha Buddha. This single thought alone is my original teacher; this single thought alone—
This is precisely the transformation Buddha. This single thought-moment is the fierce general who destroys hell;
this single thought-moment is the precious sword that slays all depravities; this single thought-moment is the bright lamp that opens up the darkness;
this single thought-moment is the great ship that ferries one across the sea of suffering; this single thought-moment is the excellent remedy for escaping birth and death. This single...
This single thought-moment is the path for exiting the triple world. This very thought-moment is the original-nature Amitābha.
This very thought-moment reaches the Pure Land of Mind-Only. It is sufficient simply to remember this one phrase, "Amitābha Buddha," keeping it in mind so as not to lose it.
Let every thought-moment constantly manifest before you; let every thought-moment never depart from the mind. Even when there is nothing to do, it is thus.
This is mindfulness. One is mindful of circumstances in this way; one is mindful of peace and happiness in this way; one is mindful of the suffering of illness in this way;
one is mindful of birth in this way; and one is mindful of death in this way. When one is mindful in this manner, clearly and without confusion, why then need one ask others for the path home?
*The Questions on the Pure Land by Chan Master Tianru*:

"There are many types of 'Pure Lands of Shared Residence,' yet you now specifically point to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). Furthermore, why do you single out its environment and its superior conditions for praise?
Answer: "It is precisely because of the environment and the conditions that I point specifically to it. As a sutra says: 'In that land there are no manifold sufferings;'"
They experience all manner of bliss. Now, let us compare this with the Sahā world. This physical body of flesh and blood—birth for it is entirely suffering;

those born by transformation from lotuses have no suffering of birth. Here, as the seasons change and pass, decay and aging daily encroach; there, cold and heat do not shift, and thus there is no suffering of aging.
Here, the four elements are difficult to harmonize, giving rise to many illnesses and ailments; there, the transformed body is subtle and wondrous.
There is no suffering of illness; such people of seventy years are rare. There is no suffering of impermanence; their lifespan is immeasurable. There is no suffering of death; they do not die.
There is no suffering of separation from loved ones; they have no affectionate attachments to kin. There is no suffering of being parted from those one loves;
they have no parents, wives, or children. There is no suffering of meeting enemies and foes; there is no enmity, for they gather with the most excellent assembly. There is no hatred or resentment.
This [state] is suffering. Here, one is tormented by hunger and cold, and craving never finds satisfaction; there, clothing, food, and precious jewels are all received as already perfected.
Here, this physical form is ugly and defiled, with many sense faculties impaired or deformed; there, the appearance is upright and majestic, all endowed with radiance.

Here, one revolves through birth and death; there, one eternally realizes non-arising. Here, there are the sufferings of the four realms of existence; there, even the names of the three evil paths do not exist. This...

Hills and mounds form ravines and pits; thorns and brambles grow into forests; mountains of earth and stone are filled with filth and impurity. There, the ground is made of gold and jewel-trees reach toward the heavens;
pavilions soar with the seven treasures and flowers bloom in four colors. Here, the Twin Śāla Trees have already perished and the Dragon Flower Tree has not yet arrived;
there, the Honored One Amitāyus currently preaches the Dharma. Here, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are but objects of our reverent admiration for their noble names.
In that realm, those boundless superiors personally act as supreme friends; here, these hordes of demons and externalists disturb right practice.
In that Buddha-land, transformation brings unified governance, and demons and externalists leave no trace; here, seductive forms and licentiousness delude practitioners.

In that land, the retribution of the pure is such that there are truly no women; here, evil beasts and malevolent spirits spread perverse sounds together. In that realm, the water-birds and forest trees all...
In proclaiming the sublime Dharma, the conditions and environments of the two lands differ vastly; yet, the excellence of the Land of Bliss (Sukhāvatī) is not easily exhausted in description.
Its environment is supreme, capable of gathering sentient beings who aspire to attain purity. Its conditions are supreme, capable of assisting those born there in the power of their practice.
It is from this that one attains the three non-regressions in their perfection. Compared to other pure abodes, there is a distinct difference in terms of ascent and descent.
Question: In this world of the five turbidities, all people possess transgressions. Even if one has not committed the five heinous crimes, who among us is free from other karmic offenses?
If these have not been repented and extinguished, can one achieve rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha’s name at the moment of death? Answer: One may indeed attain rebirth.
This is entirely due to the inconceivable power of Amitābha’s great vows. As stated in the *Nāgasena Bhikṣu Sūtra*: "A hundred large..."
If a stone is placed upon a boat, it does not sink because it relies on the power of the boat; yet without the boat, even a small stone will sink.

The boat is a metaphor for the power of the Buddha, and the stone is a metaphor for evil karma. Therefore, there is the teaching of "rebirth while carrying one's karma," whereby those possessed of afflictions and defilements can attain birth in the Pure Land of Shared Dwelling.
Seng Xiongjun was a native of Bingzhou and Fenzhou; he worked as a butcher of oxen. At the time of his death, he saw a herd of oxen.

His skull was pressed down, and his agony was excruciating. Zhang Zhonggui made his living by killing chickens. At the moment of his death, he saw a divine being drive a flock of chickens that pecked out both his eyes;
blood flowed until it filled his bed. By invoking the name of the Buddha, he was reborn together with them in the Pure Land.

How could this be anything other than the power of the Buddha? To clarify this further through analogy: it is like a person who has committed a crime and should be imprisoned by the authorities, yet seeks refuge with a king. Upon receiving [the king's protection],...

The King issued an edict summoning officials, yet they could not detain him as he returned to the imperial capital. He provided funds for his journey west, saying: "That one may be born in the Pure Land is due to the power of others;
it is through the grasping of Amitābha’s vow, the encouragement and praise of Śākyamuni, and the protective mindfulness of all Buddhas. It is like crossing a great ocean:
having obtained a massive ship, and moreover a skilled guide, if one is further aided by a favorable wind, one will surely reach the other shore with speed. If one is unwilling [to accept this],...
Boarding the boat, one lingers in a wretched land; whose fault is this? Question:

The human mind is easily advancing and easily retreating. Upon hearing a single word of exhortation, one becomes courageous and diligent; yet, suddenly encountering obstacles and difficulties, the mind immediately turns away.
Everyone then says that the practice of Pure Land is a matter for after death, offering no benefit or aid in the present moment. This is not to be wondered at.
Is that so? [The Master] replied: "Your vision is not yet broad. By upholding the names of the Buddhas, one obtains ten benefits:
first, throughout the day and night, all the devas and powerful divine generals, with retinues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will protect you while remaining invisible;
second, twenty-five great bodhisattvas, such as Avalokiteśvara and others, along with all other bodhisattvas, will constantly follow and protect you; third, all the Buddhas..."
Day and night they shall be protected by mindfulness; Amitābha will constantly emit light to embrace them. First, none of the four classes of evil spirits can harm them.

Second, venomous snakes, poisonous dragons, and toxic drugs shall all fail to take effect. Third, fire, water, enemies, thieves, swords, arrows, imprisonment, shackles, and untimely death—all these shall not befall them.
Fourth, their past karma shall be extinguished, and those with whom they have karmic enmity shall find liberation; no further adversaries shall remain to confront them.
Seventh, dreams for seven nights will be upright; one may see the sublime and wondrous form of Amitābha.
Eighth, the mind is constantly joyful, the complexion is radiant, physical strength is abundant, and all actions are auspicious.

Ninth, one is always respectfully honored and provided for by all the people of the world, who joyfully prostrate before one as they would before a Buddha. Tenth, at the end of life, there is no fear, and right mindfulness manifests before one.
One shall behold the holy assembly of Amitābha, who, holding golden lotus flowers, will welcome one to be reborn there. Until the end of the future, one shall experience supreme and wondrous bliss.
These ten benefits, as recorded in detail within the sutras and proclaimed from the Buddha’s own mouth, bring benefit both in this life and in future lives.
One need only apply oneself with diligence; there is no need for doubt.
Question: The cultivation of perfect contemplation and the mindfulness of the mind-only seem to be the practice-gates for those of superior capacity.

The ten vows of the *Avataṃsaka* and the ten minds of the *Ratnakūṭa* are likewise the functional application of those with great roots. If one’s faculties do not correspond to these practices, it is difficult to achieve their merit and conduct.
Now, when I examine myself and reflect upon my own nature, I find that I can only single-mindedly hold the Name, adding prostrations and repentance. How should the Master regard me?
"What? [The Master] replied, "Excellent! You have understood the proper measure. You are fit for the teaching of exclusive practice without interruption (*mujian*).

As for 'practice without interruption,' it means that the body exclusively bows to Amitābha Buddha, the mouth exclusively recites the name of Amitābha Buddha, and the mind exclusively contemplates Amitābha Buddha.
The Venerable Shandao was traditionally regarded in India as an emanation of Amitābha; observing him now..."
It is said that the essential point lies in the continuous succession of every thought-moment. Yongming said:
"One must single-mindedly take refuge and cultivate diligently throughout one's entire life; whether sitting or lying down, always face the west.

When practicing the Way and performing prostrations, when reciting the Buddha’s name and making vows, be earnest and sincere, free from all distracting thoughts—as if facing execution, as if in prison, or as if surrounded by enemies."

Pursued by fire and water and pressed by calamities, with single-minded resolve seek salvation, praying to escape the wheel of suffering and swiftly realize non-arising, so as to extensively deliver all sentient beings, perpetuate and honor the Triple Gem, and vow to repay the four debts of gratitude. Only through such supreme sincerity will this not be in vain.
If, however, one’s words and deeds do not accord, or if faith and vows are slight, lacking a mind of continuous mindfulness and instead characterized by frequent interruptions—

Those who harbor such intentions rely on their own indolence; at the moment of death, they hope for rebirth, yet they are obstructed by karmic hindrances and will likely find it difficult to encounter virtuous friends.
Overwhelmed by the winds and fires [of dissolution], right mindfulness cannot be established. Why is this? The present is the cause and the moment of death is the effect;
if the cause is real, the effect will not be in vain. When the sound is harmonious, the resonance follows suit; when the form is upright, the shadow is straight.
Question: If worldly affairs cannot simply be cast aside, how should one deal with them? Answer:

If one truly contemplates impermanence with sincere and earnest resolve, then let them attend to public and private duties as they arise and respond to challenges from all directions; this will not hinder their practice of reciting the Buddha’s name.
As it is said: "In the morning there is Amitābha; in the evening there is Amitābha. Even if one is as busy as an arrow, [the Buddha remains present]."

"Not being separated from Amitābha" is also expressed by the saying: "Though the bamboo is dense, it does not hinder the flowing stream; though the mountain is high, how could it obstruct the flying white clouds?
Furthermore, even for those who are most preoccupied and have no leisure for even a moment, one must perform the ten recitations every morning.

If this is practiced over a long period until the merit is perfected, it will not be in vain. This is the essential method of instruction bequeathed by the former masters; you should follow and practice it accordingly.
*The Direct Pointing to Mindfulness of the Buddha through the Jewel King Samādhi*, composed by Chan Master Miaoye of Siming.

Now, the pure and the defiled share the same essence; sentient beings and Buddhas are of one principle. All dharmas are fundamentally equal—why should there be any need for exhortation to practice? Yet, alas, [sentient beings] are deluded...
The mind creates objects; thus, the distinction between the pure and the defiled arises. These are established through mutual relativity, and bondage and liberation are vastly different.

Because one remains entangled for many kalpas and finds it difficult to awaken to this truth, one must diligently exhort sentient beings in the ocean of suffering to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Once a practitioner has deeply understood that the distinctions between purity and defilement, and suffering and joy, are true and unerring, they shall proceed like a farmer seeking profit, unable to stop themselves.
Yet, farmers labor day and night without rest for the sake of a single year’s sustenance from hunger and cold, never tiring throughout the year.
