The traveler, however, transcends the sufferings of kalpas; how could it stop at the hunger and cold of a single year? To ascend to the security of the nine grades—how could it stop at the warmth and fullness of one year?

Between the two gates of subduing and gathering, they are like gold, jade, sand, and stone. Even a child of three feet in height would surely cast away the stone to seek the gold; there is no need to urge them.

Take it up yourself. That this land is suffering and that land is blissful; that this is the drowning of birth and death and that is sovereign liberation—all these can be distinguished even by a child.

One must certainly abandon the defiled and seek the pure with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire. If one hears the teaching and acts upon it immediately, what need is there for further exhortation?
These two lands of suffering and bliss were spoken of by the Buddha; believe them with certainty and without doubt, and through cultivation, you shall attain them for yourself.
When people today see excrement or a corpse, they pinch their noses, knit their brows, loathe its stench and filth, and desire to depart from it as quickly as possible.

When they see brocade or fine silks, they relax their countenances and break into smiles, craving their brilliance and purity, and desiring to obtain them as quickly as possible. They cannot endure even for a moment these illusory objects of beauty or ugliness, yet their hatred and attachment burn fiercely.
Thus, they do not swiftly give rise to joy regarding ultimate bliss nor revulsion toward ultimate suffering, even though these states will persist through long kalpas.
How extreme is this folly! How profound is this delusion! Furthermore, in this realm, Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet appeared;

the worthy sages are hidden and concealed, while sentient beings rush headlong through the sea of suffering like children who have lost their father. If one does not take the King of Vows of Ultimate Bliss as one’s refuge, who will provide protection?
Even for gods and immortals who have not yet transcended the realm of empty space, it is not easy to reach; how much less so for those of the three grades who practice the ten wholesome deeds!
The causes for being born as a deva within the three realms range from the inferior to the superior, each passing through many kalpas; yet it is especially difficult to fulfill one's aspirations.
Success is as small as a drop in the vast ocean. In the interim, one may encounter the factions of evil Māras, leading to eternal regression and total loss.

How could one dare claim to escape the three realms or hope for the four fruits and four stages of the path? This is all the more so when considering the passage through the various stages of faith, practice, abiding, and advancement—how much more difficult it is to transcend them.

Yes. If one cultivates the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, one will not remain in the stage of an ordinary person for more than one lifetime; one will cross directly through the three realms and five paths, receive the Buddha’s guidance, and attain birth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*).
Upon the blossoming of the lotus, one shall behold the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and awaken to the Way, all within a single thought-moment.
Taking vast strides toward the Great Vehicle, one shall make offerings to all the Triple Gem and transform all sentient beings. When Maitreya is born, [one shall] once again...

Having come to this place, you instruct all those who have been your parents, wives, children, brothers, sisters, enemies, and kin throughout kalpas in the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), and inform them of their past causes, causing them all to realize the fruits [of the path]. How, then, could your conduct and vows not be vast and great?
Such meritorious virtues, if lost through a single moment of negligence in practice, will belong to future lives. How could one afford to be lax?
Moreover, worldly affairs are manifold and continuous like an unbroken chain; the mind does not abide for even a single thought-moment, and the body never rests wherever it goes.
These serve to cause my rise and fall and obstruct my original nature. From kalpa after kalpa until now, there has been no respite; impermanence and change cannot endure long.
Stay. Even a lifespan of a hundred years does not exceed the snap of a finger. Today and tomorrow, one cannot guarantee survival.

Suddenly, when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, one is unaware that in an instant one has been reborn as a different being, receiving a form according to the causes of one's karma—be it with fur and horns, walking upon the earth or flying through the air.
All understanding of today is forgotten; one wanders in a daze through the three miserable realms and six paths of existence, drifting aimlessly for many lifetimes.
Eons pass, yet one does not know where one will return. Even if Maitreya were to appear in the world, what certainty would there be regarding my place of birth?
I have not even heard the names of my parents or the Triple Gem, let alone the complete teachings of the scriptures. Though I receive various forms of existence, I cherish them with deep attachment.
From karma I produce further karma; from darkness I enter into deeper darkness. My fear of death and craving for life are no different from today. If I do not achieve liberation in this very moment—
In the interim, emulating those previously awakened great men, he vigorously gave rise to the Great Mind and established a resolute will.
Summoning the power to lift a cauldron or pull up a mountain, he severed [all bonds] in a single stroke. How could his practice not then become manifest, its radiance moving gods and humans?

All beings received his grace, and all Buddhas held him in their protective mindfulness. The three evil realms were closed, and the gate of *dhāraṇī* was opened; he did not have to wait for his retribution in this Sahā world to be exhausted.

Thus, one attains rebirth there. If, however, one waits for a place that is secure and convenient, where food and clothing are abundant, where incense and flowers are plentiful, and where every matter accords with one's wishes—calculating past and future, divining an auspicious time, and settling both debts of gratitude and resentment to perfect a virtuous deed—[one will fail].
Only then does one set forth in practice. Even if the realm of empty space were exhausted, there would be no end to this [practice].

One who is diligent is not discouraged by the eight winds of the world, nor by physical or mental afflictions, nor by various views, nor by the causes of great or small illnesses that might cause them to slacken their practice.
When a practitioner wishes to enter samādhi, they may therein encounter all manner of forceful or gentle [obstacles].
Regarding the two types of māras that cause internal and external confusion:
you should firm up your resolve and redouble your diligence so that it is indestructible like a vajra-banner, immovable like Mount Sumeru, and unassailable by any poison like the great ocean.
Even if a Buddha were to say, "You shall not attain birth [in the Pure Land]," you should immediately reply: "I have already received the prediction from Śākyamuni Buddha that all sentient beings..."
All who are born [in this world] should make a vow: "I vow to be born in that land. This applies even to those who do not cease from the ten evil deeds or the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).

As for me, I shall not commit the five heinous crimes; if I recite the name ten times or more, I shall certainly attain birth there. How could the Buddha deceive himself, or would he ever be willing to violate his original vow?
Moreover, the Buddhas of the ten directions have extended their broad and long tongues to testify to this matter. Therefore, one must surely seek birth there and never regress. This is...
For the practitioner, this is the vajra-like strength of the extended banner of valor;

even the Buddha’s prophecy cannot cause one to retreat from their initial resolve, let alone the evil factions of Māras, the realms of water, fire, thieves, and powerful heterodoxies, or the passions for wives and concubines—how could these move my practice and vows?
Someone asks: "If worldly people practice yet do not attain birth [in the Pure Land], why is this? The answer is: "Their views differ, and thus their practices differ."
"It is not dignified. In that case, would their merit be lost in vain? Answer: "They must certainly rely upon the power of Amitābha’s vows.

If they are not born [in the Pure Land] in this life, they will certainly be born in the second life; if not in the second life, they will certainly be born in the third life. With a single thought of turning toward him, one will surely attain birth in the future.
This is called 'all are non-retrogressive. It is only that they undergo the suffering of saṃsāra in vain for many kalpas."
One must resolve upon this for the rest of one's life; how could one allow their will to be divided, thereby falling into the state of those who seek rebirth in another world?
Furthermore, there is the "Ten Recitations Dharma Gate" of Ciyun: every morning, after washing and rinsing the mouth, one should practice in a quiet place facing west.

This is the primary cause for rebirth and must not be lost. Someone may ask: "How does one apply the mind so that it does not become distracted? The answer is: by being able to direct the body [toward the West].

Regarding the mindfulness of the mouth: do not concern yourself with its scattering, provided it is not interrupted; one will naturally become single-minded, which may itself be termed "single-mindedness.
The only measure is to practice without ceasing; thus, there is no need to worry about distraction. It is like a mother who has lost her beloved child.
The dragon lost its life-essence pearl; it was not that it expected the mind to become one, but it became one spontaneously—how could it have been forced to become one?
That the mind cannot be forcibly controlled depends truly upon whether the practitioner is diligent or indolent.
The Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection is called "the Single Practice" (*ekayāna*). All mundane and supramundane auxiliary practices for the path are cultivated solely for the sake of the Pure Land;
there are no divergent paths. Just as all rivers flowing into the ocean collectively receive the name "ocean," so too do the myriad virtues converge here and are thus named the "Single Practice.
Therefore, all the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, faculties, powers, factors of awakening, and the path; the Four Great Vows and the Six Perfections—all [are included therein].

Regarding practices for the Pure Land: even a single act of goodness as brief as a finger-snap, or mindfulness of the Buddha with a distracted mind; a single recitation of the name, a single raising of the hands, a single prostration, recitation, or gazing upon the image;
a single offering of incense, water, a flower, or a lamp; a single article of worship; or from one thought-moment up to ten thought-moments;
or a single act of giving, a single precept, or a single practice of patience; or meditative concentration and wisdom—all such virtuous manifestations are dedicated toward the Ultimate [Pure Land].
Joy. By the power of their vows, although there may be differences in speed, all shall attain rebirth. It is like drops of water deposited in the ocean;

though they pass through many kalpas, they are not destroyed, lost, altered, or exhausted. Likewise, by dedicating even small roots of goodness toward the Land of Ultimate Bliss, although one passes through the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), those roots of goodness are neither lost, destroyed, nor exhausted—provided that one excludes those of the heretical lineage and those whose causal mind has not yet [turned].
To rise [from practice] while wholesome conduct is not yet established and body and mind are not yet subdued—those who expect a response before this point cannot be spoken of in the same breath.

Therefore, among the samādhis and liberations, the practices and vows, the dhāraṇīs, and the immeasurable Dharma gates, only the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha encompasses them all perfectly without exception, fully complete in every way.
It is like the great ocean swallowing all streams, its nature neither increasing nor decreasing; it is like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Because its essence fulfills all wishes without deficiency, it is also called the "Treasure King Samādhi. By means of this samādhi, the World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly.
Among those of great capacity, such as Mañjuśrī and others, as well as the three vehicles and the eight classes of beings, there were none who did not incline their hearts [toward it].
When the Dharma flowed eastward to the land, it was propagated on Mount Lu; the hopes of the world all praised its teaching. From that time...

From the time of the Buddha until the present day, there have been sages and worthies, eminent monks and great scholars, who either practiced it themselves and exhorted others, or composed writings and made vows.
They valued the Dharma as they would a treasure and regarded their own bodies as mere dust; casting aside all hesitation, they established their conduct and strove with might to cultivate this path.

The arrayed constellations and sands of the Ganges cannot serve as a metaphor for their vastness. If even one who lacks faith may still be born in the borderlands, how much more so for those who practice correctly?
Even if one were to separately cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) relying solely on one's own power, there would be the peril of regression and being possessed by demons.
However, if one relies upon the Buddha’s power to practice, success is certain; demonic activities will no longer arise, and one shall never again regress. Furthermore, this samādhi is not...

They will remain far removed from demons; all officials, verbal disputes, matters of right and wrong, calamities, water and fire, thieves, bandits, evil people, and ominous events—even tigers, wolves, insects, and beasts, as well as ghosts, specters, and inauspicious occurrences—will be unable to inflict harm upon them.
Furthermore, they shall not be afflicted by any epidemics, dysentery, smallpox, carbuncles, scabies, or the various ailments of the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue associated with lowly conditions.
May vows and practices remain unimpaired; all other obstacles can be dispelled.

However, as for fame, gain, and offerings—the sweet, affectionate, and soft thieves—as well as anger and the fire of anger, even with the power of the Buddha, one cannot be saved from them. Practitioners must apply profound diligence to repel them.
A single moment of negligence will surely lead to their being robbed [of their progress]. Yet these "soft" demons only harm those of shallow faith who are greedy, lazy, and forgetful of mindfulness.
As for such a person, their vigor is like a fierce fire that becomes even more intense upon meeting water; how could they dare to approach slightly and cast a sidelong glance [at worldly things]?

This body is protected and assisted by devas and humans. At the time of death, they attain right mindfulness and are reborn in the Pure Land. Celestial music fills the sky, extraordinary fragrances pervade the chamber, radiant light illuminates the body, and a jeweled throne appears before them.
Amitābha welcomes them with his arm and the Bodhisattvas receive them with their hands; they know the time of their passing in advance.
Upon reaching right mindfulness, his various obstructions suddenly vanished. He bathed, sat in the full lotus posture, and preached the Dharma to the assembled multitude.

Joining his palms, he took his leave; at times, he further exhorted others to advance on the Path. He wrote a verse, cast down his pen, and passed away with palms joined. After his death, his entire body remained as if alive.
His teeth, bones, and prayer beads were not consumed by the fire when burned; the flames were extraordinary, brilliant in five colors, and auspicious.
Objects hovered in the air without dispersing, and wherever the smoke reached, śarīra-relics flowed like pearls; these are things commonly witnessed by the ears and eyes of the present age.
Yet, that they are not so in ordinary times is because one has not clearly practiced them through the power of pure diligence. Alas!
That people today practice without effect is because their roots of faith are shallow and thin, and because their ground is not true; they have never established their conduct beforehand.
Desiring others to know their inner state, they outwardly display themselves with ostentation, wishing to appear radiant so as to elicit the respect of others and hope for some gain;
this even leads them to falsely claim that they have beheld pure realms, or seen minor visions, or auspicious signs in dreams, without being able to discern whether these are true or false.
First, I wish to clarify that those who are base and inferior will inevitably be deluded by Māra, causing their vows and practices to degenerate and fall into the realms of birth and death;
how can they not be cautious! Although there may be rituals for the *dojō*, if they are known by others, it is truly unavoidable;

yet, how could one intentionally expose such traces and cause the ruin of one's contemplative practice? One must instead examine oneself with discernment and practice in secret and in reality, harboring [the truth] within.
One must possess a sense of shame and remorse; do not reveal one's virtues. If there are latent obstacles within that one wishes to extinguish, auspicious signs may appear faintly.

If one does not conceal these virtues so that they reach the ears of others, one’s conduct will surely be compromised. Master Huiyuan beheld sacred manifestations three times, yet he never spoke of them during his ordinary days.

Only at the moment of death is it otherwise. I pray most earnestly, I pray most earnestly. Furthermore, although the essential nature of this samādhi is perfect, one should exhaustively observe its subtle regulations and reform all vulgar failings;
even regarding minor transgressions, one should harbor great fear. Thus, one understands and follows the Mahāyāna.
One practices based on the "Small Vehicle" (Hīnayāna) and is thus able to harmonize with this samādhi. The "Small" is not inherently small; the Small follows along until understanding is perfected.

Perfection does not depart from the Small; the Small is itself both small and great. When understanding and practice are of one principle without division, one transcends worldly views. As the Sūtra says:

"Filially support one's parents, serve one's teachers and elders, maintain a compassionate heart and refrain from killing, cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, and receive and uphold the Three Refuges."

Be fully endowed with the various precepts. Do not violate the rules of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*). Generate the bodhicitta. Have deep faith in cause and effect. Do not slander the Mahāyāna. Encourage those who practice.
Each of the above phrases constitutes a single dharma-practice. The ancients each had a chapter of dharma-instructions. Furthermore, one must protect the minds of others;
do not allow them to harbor boastfulness or resentment. Remain composed and natural in all movements and activities. Recite Mahāyāna sūtras and understand the foremost [truth].
Principle: Associate with virtuous friends and inquire of those who have awakened. Do not cling to your own views, nor boast of your own strengths.
Set your will upon forbearance; your conduct should rely upon the sutras. Listen to the True Dharma and do not disparage the monastics.

Cease worldly, miscellaneous virtues and do not crave fame or profit. Stay far removed from evil and be loyal in all affairs. Take faults upon yourself and strictly admonish against frivolous speech. With a single mind, do not...
One should regard all people as Buddhas, renounce worldly skills and talents, and seek only rebirth in the Pure Land with a body that is necessarily pure.
All such immeasurable virtuous practices should be cultivated; they can assist the Right Path and further sever the defiled mind of the world.

Regarding objects of hatred and love, one will encounter no obstacles; with the mind concentrated as one, one will certainly be born in the Pure Land. The merit of this is exceedingly great and cannot [be measured].
I have fully recounted these secret practices; though they are sublime, those who have attained rebirth there remain unnamed, for how could one know their number?
Those whose names are recorded in biographies are like mere drops in the great ocean.

Yet, if a person relies upon these instructions, they can still benefit immeasurable sentient beings burdened by karmic enmity—let alone their own parents, teachers, spiritual kin, siblings, and even their peers.

Those who daily deliver me from affliction and hardship, and who have uplifted me, shall not fail to receive their reward; yet one need only cultivate this practice, for there is no kindness that will not be requited.
Amitābha Buddha and the two Great Beings dwell in a realm of profound depth; within the sea of suffering, it is difficult to draw near to them and difficult to keep them in mind.
Yet those who are able to maintain mindfulness of them will surely attain liberation. As the Sūtra says: "Merely hearing the name of the Buddha... (The second part is incomplete).
The name of the Bodhisattva eliminates the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas; how much more so when one recollects it! This person is a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among humanity.
With Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta as their supreme friends, they shall sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and be born into the family of all Buddhas.

Therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions display their great wheels of tongues to earnestly exhort and encourage them, and the Teacher of the Sahā world issues his instructions with repeated admonition.
The words were fervent and urgent: "Sentient beings of the five turbidities must surely cultivate this path to attain deliverance from the world.

For in those five turbidities, body and mind are both in suffering, and they take suffering as their very life, like a confluence of fire and water. Yet the Buddha, precisely within such suffering, exercises his compassion most deeply.
From the time the World-Honored One attained perfect enlightenment until his entry into *nirvāṇa*, his voice remained non-dual for all who possess consciousness."

This current must be engraved upon one's very flesh and bones. The Vow-power of Amitābha has never lacked for followers throughout the ages. Sages have proclaimed it before, and worthies have followed after;

it has spread vast and clear throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, pouring down abundantly upon the six destinies and the four modes of birth. Celestial deities turned toward its transformation, and spirits and ghosts submitted to it.
These deeds are recorded in practice and fully contained within the canonical statutes, overflowing the ocean-treasury and the dragon palaces, and spreading everywhere.
Whether among humans or in the heavens, all this is brought about by the power of my vow, Amitābha. The Buddha said:
"In the final evil age, when my Dharma is extinguished, only these scriptural teachings shall remain for many hundreds of years to deliver all sentient beings. Thus, as for this Dharma:
Is this not the ultimate instruction for us who follow behind? Eight times eight winged birds fall into ignorance;

they follow others in calling out names, and lotuses grow upon their tongues. Can a human being truly be inferior to a bird? I was born in the final age, five hundred years after [the Buddha’s passing]. Human faculties are shallow and thin;
people harbor doubts and lack faith, holding various divergent views and erroneous interpretations, each clinging to their own differences. This is the state of correct practice.
Such people are frequently deluded and confused, their hearts filled with sorrow and grief.

For this reason, I have collected various texts from my teachings on Chan and Pure Land, extracting their most profound and essential meanings to compose this work. Arranged into a coherent volume, it is now circulated throughout the world.

Repudiating the heterodox and manifesting the orthodox, I universally pray that all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm may, upon hearing this teaching, attain understanding through a single insight;

realize their true mind, know that Amitābha’s environment and inhabitants reside within the Western Land, and realize that the environment and inhabitants of the West do not depart from one's own original nature.

May all sentient beings indeed ascend the profound stages. Furthermore, I pray that those who have first awakened will not begrudge their compassion; seeing those who have not yet realized the truth, may they instruct them according to the Dharma.
If a person remains obscured, may you analyze the subtle and profound according to their faculties and their ailments, and proclaim the teaching once more for their sake.
If one can attain faith and understanding for even a single moment, their vows will surely be fulfilled and rebirth [in the Pure Land] may be expected; the merit thereof is beyond description.

Even if one’s heterodox attachments are firm and their faith and joy are not deep, yet if a single phrase colors the spirit, it becomes a causal seed that will bring benefit through successive generations, inexhaustible and infinite.
If one can take no teacher other than the mind, being neither deceptive nor false, and follow this orthodox teaching to instruct others—

As for those who are weary: even if they do not practice themselves, it shall be as if they have practiced; even if they have not yet studied themselves, it shall be as if they have studied. Why is this?

Because the Dharma-realm has a single characteristic, being devoid of self and other. In the past, there was a person who twice dedicated his own possessions to establish an assembly and exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name.

Upon the end of his life, he was reborn in the Pure Land; the account of this is well known. This is able to give rise to a heart of compassion and demonstrates the power of gathering and sustaining beings.
Regarding these signs, as well as the ability to benefit others and encourage them toward mindfulness, the merit obtained is vast and great. One is acting as an emissary of the Dharma King;
however, one must not cling to the notion that it is unnecessary to practice for oneself. The gateways of the Dharma are like the ocean—how could they ever be fully described?
I have merely recorded what I have heard to inspire and encourage the world.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss is most pure; its adornments are subtle and wondrous, transcending the world.

Amitābha’s power of vows is equal to space, and his marks, signs, and radiance are likewise so. Moment by moment, he does not depart from the realm of sentient beings; may he universally deliver us all to birth in that land.
We ourselves have willingly remained within the cycle of birth and death, sinking and wallowing through kalpas without transcendence. That Buddha now extends his arm—

I have waited for a long time; my sighs and the snapping of my fingers have been most earnest. The light is about to manifest and the lotus is opening. Now is precisely the right time; I pray to be reborn there.
The body is subject to impermanence and the time is passing away. Tormented by the convergence of manifold sufferings, one ought to depart from them.
I pray that you will quickly recollect the Buddha and practice together with me, so that at the end of this retribution-body, we may be born in Sukhāvatī.
Verses on the Pure Land from the Western Studio, composed by Chan Master Chushi of Siming:
"The true body of our Buddha is immeasurable; Great beings attend him with radiant splendor; At the time of eating, all are celestial delicacies."

In the places where the meal is taken, there is nothing that is not a sacred site; beneath the courtyard, the azure stream softly utters its melody, and before the hall, the jade-like grasses delicately waft their fragrance.
The adornments of the lands of the ten directions are all equal, yet it is said that the Western Quarter is distinct from other regions.
Constantly entangled by the sufferings of this Sahā world, I hear only of the Pure Land and seek nothing else there.

Gods and humans are all vessels for the Mahāyāna; even the grasses and trees bear the names of the Triple Gem. In every garden, patterns emerge like embroidery; tier upon tier of pavilions appear as if spontaneously formed.
O worthy ones, do not wonder why I return so late; I have heard it said that the lotuses have only now begun to bloom.

Looking back, the precious realm of golden lotuses lies afar; Pavilions and terraces stand one by one, leaning against the clouds and sky. The warbling of yellow orioles is beautiful, as spring remains forever;
The branches of the jade trees are supple, never withering through the years. Flowing waters have sound as they turn along the banks; Countless lovely flowers drift on the wind.
On the day the rustic returns of his own accord, Why wait for the worthy ones to summon him with folded notes?
Formed through paper paintings, wood carvings, and clay sculptures, the manifest true Buddha appears with great clarity.

Taking refuge is not the business of another; merit and virtue arise from within oneself. When ten thousand trees bloom, it is because the earth is warm; when a thousand rivers reflect the moon, it is because the waves are clear.
Morning prostrations and evening salutations should always be thus; everywhere one goes, one enters the City of Ultimate Bliss.
Above the pond, lotus flowers bloom; upon them stands a person. The Buddha’s light shines upon his purple-gold body, and as he hears the wondrous Dharma, the defilements of his mind are cleansed.
He rescues all deluded beings from the wheel of suffering; with every step, he travels through lands as numerous as motes of dust.
To benefit sentient beings, he shall ultimately fulfill the cause of *nirvāṇa*. In this Sahā world, time passes swiftly; how many kalpas of spring must pass in Sukhāvatī?
This single body is but a floating bubble, a dream, or an illusion; how can you merely indulge in greed and anger? You should seek the direct path of practice;
do not emulate those who are foolish and heedless. Guarding the precepts is as pure as ice and snow; setting the mind right is essential for intimacy with the sages and worthies.
Clearly pointing out the sun flying westward, those with true discernment are led to realize their original nature.
Pointing afar toward my hometown at the setting sun, a single path of return is as straight as a bowstring. In the sky, melodies play every kind of music; upon the water, blossoms open like lotuses.
The branches and stems of various trees become a hundred jewels; our communal dwelling and sustenance surpass those of the devas.
My Master, if you have a vow, please grant me your acceptance; let not my thirty years of diligent devotion be in vain.
A single lotus holds a holy embryo; when a lifetime’s merit is perfected, a flower blooms. Necklaces of jewels appear according to one’s mind;
vessels of *sudhā* arrive with every thought. The golden palace has radiance that swallows sun and moon; the jade tower has no room for dust.
The Dharma King speaks the True Reality for me, until even empty space smiles to its cheeks.
Having established karmic conditions in the Pure Land, these thoughts manifest throughout the two periods of six watches.

As dusk falls, my wholesome thoughts increase; I follow the setting sun as it descends the vast sky. The Tathāgata’s precious hand personally strokes my crown; the Great Being’s golden body seems to brush against my shoulder.
Without relying on a womb, this illusory form is formed; within my own home, there is naturally the lotus of the Jade Pond.
How pitiable are these turbid and evil sentient beings! When will the fruit of the Bodhi path be perfected? It is said in general that the land is purified according to the mind;
yet how can one’s physical form and spirit not be dragged away by karma? When the true sword is brandished, the vines fall from the tree;
when the clouds of delusion disperse, the sun flows across the sky. Space is ultimately without obstruction; the Pure Land flows forth before one's very eyes.
About to enter this Dharma assembly and pay homage to the Golden Immortal, I gradually follow the fragrant breeze out from the precious lotus. The red *uṣṇīṣa* radiates its light without end;
the purple-gold body reflects boundlessly. Layer upon layer, jeweled nets hang down to level ground; one by one, flower pedestals reach toward the distant heavens.
Among the realms of all Buddhas, such rare wonders are as clearly revealed before me as in a bright mirror.
Coarse objects appear before one yet remain unrecognized; how often has one known that which lies beyond the Dharmakāya?

Alas, in those moments of turning the head or twisting the brain, one mistakenly identifies the time of offering incense and choosing firewood. Six characters are transmitted from mouth to ear; between the holy and the mundane, not even a single thread of silk separates them.
The True Buddha of daily life stands majestic and manifest; even to turn the light back in haste is already too late.
An inch of time is an inch of gold. I urge you to recite the Buddha’s name and quickly turn your heart back [to the Dharma].

Even if one holds the nobility of the Phoenix Pavilion and Dragon Tower, one cannot escape the encroachment of crow-like skin and crane-like hair. While the incense smoke within the cauldron has not yet dispersed, the celestial carriage in the void has already arrived from afar.
Though every dust mote and every world-system is pure, the Vow-Power of Amitābha alone is profound.
The golden countenance and white hair-bristles are but a span away; how could it be in vain to recite His name alone? At dawn, hold ten thousand recitations as the sun rises;
at night, perform a thousand chants as the moon ascends high. Through years of shifting heat and cold, never grow weary; the True Parents and their children shall surely meet.
How can one describe the myriad sufferings of this Sahā world, as numerous as the bristles on a porcupine?
A boat of compassion floats upon the bitter sea of Sahā; can it carry one from this shore to the other? To point directly at the source of delusion, one must recite the Buddha’s name;

crossing the surging waves by a direct path, one avoids being swept away by the current. For a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas there will be eternal peace and security; the five realms and three miserable paths shall all come to rest.
Even if one’s own body is of the lowest of the low grade, it is still superior to the nobility and wealth of those in Jambudvīpa.
A hundred years of human life—rarely does one reach seventy. Looking back upon past events, they are all seen as mistaken. Every time I weep for my fellow stream-enterers, where have they gone?
I idly cast aside the Pure Land and do not think of returning. Fragrant clouds form before the emerald steps; numinous birds fly amidst the coral trees.
Having realized the Dharma-body, there is no illness or affliction; moreover, partaking in the joy of Zen, hunger is forever forgotten.

Speaking of impermanence, all worldly affairs are trivial; hungry, I eat; thirsty, I drink; I am weary of busy toil. With a single mind, never retreating, I contemplate the Land of Peaceful Nurturing;
with myriad virtues practiced together, I remember Yongming. Thoroughly cleansing my prayer beads, I replace the threads; I firmly maintain the Buddha’s name without ceasing its sound.
Forgetting conditions, I let them vanish like drifting petals; I stroll idly before the wind and beneath the moon.
Long have I wandered like a drifting gourd south of Jambudvīpa, leaning upon my tower and sighing as the moon grows slender. From afar I know the assembly of Dharma is surrounded by devas;
with focused mind, I contemplate the Flower Altar adorned with a hundred jewels. This realm is like a fish in scant water, barely living like a swallow’s nest beneath the eaves.
My virtuous companions dwelling here should harbor thoughts of me: the stupa has already been built, yet it lacks its crowning pinnacle.

In a mere moment, youth turns to old age and decay; one must believe that impermanence urges us on day and night. Through the false wisdom of the ninety-six heterodox schools, one undergoes saṃsāra for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
If one does not maintain the thought of the jeweled realm and its flower ponds, how can the mountains of knives and trees of swords be destroyed?
Only by purifying one’s own mind can one give rise to the aspiration and joy that allows the sages and worthies therein to grant one their company.
In this weary life, how much time remains? Health lasts but a brief moment before illness invades; one constantly fears the floating clouds will obscure the setting sun.
One must prepare a pure dwelling and study like those of East Lin. How pitiable are the ignorant and deluded folk of the world, who do not equal the wise birds among the flowers.
Even the precious trees can discourse on the wondrous Dharma; what prevents one from sitting and listening instead of wandering in search?
The land of Sukhāvatī is praised without end; it is not the same as the realms of other Buddhas. A hundred flavors, both sweet and sour, forever fill the bowl;

the body is light and agile, able to roam through space at will. From the first thought-moment, one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); though still bound by all fetters, one can teach others the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
From antiquity to the present, records have been handed down throughout worlds as numerous as dust motes and sands, fanning the true wind of the Dharma everywhere.
When the water is warm or cool, the moon first appears; the golden countenance and Buddha-form manifest within my mind.

The spring breeze cannot easily revive withered wood, and the magnet can hardly attract a bent needle. Having failed to attain rebirth, my karmic obstacles are heavy; I shall surely expect accomplishment through deep application of effort.
It is like the power of the nine-times-transformed cinnabar: a single drop can cause iron to turn into gold.
The merit of deep mindfulness of the Buddha naturally erases transgressions; one’s body returns to dwell within the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

There, the groves and trees are joined by jade and crystal, while the great earth, mountains, and rivers unfold like brocade. Once one has taken a step from the Fragrant Realm, precious lotuses spontaneously blossom at the first opening of their flowers.
The radiant white tuft and golden countenance are such that neither heaven nor the human world can compare.
Morning and evening, within the heart of the Way; year after year, the Buddha-work remains the same.
Advancing steadily toward the realm of peace and bliss, one pays homage at the Palace of the Dharma King six times each day. One does not weary of the black smoke of incense from the square robe;
how could the red sweat on one’s hands hinder the sitting mat? How many such renunciants remain today? Only those who clearly recognize the true Master.
The Lotus Palace lies just at the western end of the house; it is easy to reach, yet no one applies their mind to its cultivation.

The Three Sages together fulfill the ocean of their compassionate vows, while I stand alone by the evening sun on the tower. On the autumn steps, the *wutong* leaves fall easily; in the night ravine, the *zuo-meng* boat is hard to conceal.
Fortunately, there are still wild ducks and geese in the Jade Pond; calling to one another, they come and go as they please.

The thousands of sutras and myriad treatises do not falsely point the way; together they indicate the single path to the West. Moment by moment, scrub and polish the mind until its defilements are purified;

from time to time, guard against the sprouts of the Way being scorched. Dwelling in the lotus of tranquil awakening, the body is secure and at ease; upon attaining the fruit, the thunderous proclamation shakes the very earth.
Do not waste your efforts calculating the *jiǎzǐ* cycle; in this Sahā world, a great kalpa is but a single morning.
Recently, someone returned from the Pure Land. In the heart of a pond, a single jade lotus had blossomed;

upon its very calyx was inscribed their name, and before their physical body, they had already formed a holy embryo. In the blissful leisure of Sukhāvatī, one lives forever without death; in this world of Jambudvīpa, the pressing constraints are most pitiable.
The Dharma King has specially bestowed his compassionate grace, so that we may sit together upon a golden terrace a hundred feet high.
I myself recite the Buddha’s name and practice dhyāna; I rejoice that my square robe and crown-protuberance are complete.

Having cultivated the fruits of merit through many lifetimes, I have now established the karmic conditions of incense according to the nine grades. My name, [insert name], is inscribed within the deep folds of the flower; I dream of being beside the long star and the setting moon.
The turbid, evil ordinary person and the pure Buddha—these two pearls, black and white, are threaded together upon a single string.

When mindfulness reaches its limit and the mind opens to behold the Buddha, one naturally arrives at the emerald lotus pond. Through thousands upon thousands of kalpas, the sins of the wheel of fire are purified;
from the jade trees, light radiates in tens of millions of branches. Deep conversations with virtuous friends never grow weary, and the wondrous speech of the numinous birds is truly beyond thought.
When merit is accomplished and fruition is complete in a mere moment, even a rushing torrent or a flash of lightning seems slow by comparison.
Boundless Great Beings and Śrāvakas—how could this vast assembly not be divided chapter by chapter? The sages of this single assembly remain eternally in samādhi;

those coming and going from the ten directions all travel upon clouds. They discuss the profound mystery beneath the trees where mani-jewels drip like water; they recite the Buddha’s name amidst the groves among the *saṃjīva* birds.
Whether sitting, reclining, or walking, they encounter no obstruction; heavenly flowers fall in profusion wherever they go.
Devas and humans alike all realize spiritual powers; each possesses the same golden hue and marks.

They perform Buddha-work by scattering myriad wondrous flowers, while fragrant winds arise throughout worlds as numerous as dust motes and sands. When their bodies are touched by the light of his form, they become supple and soft.
Musical instruments and flowing sounds proclaim suffering and emptiness. Leaning back against carved railings, they gaze upon jeweled trees; within them lie boundless Buddha-lands.
Beneath the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*, one loses the human body; how many are there who, having lost it, regain it again? Ten thousand practices are not equal to cultivating pure deeds;
why toil with a single mind over the red dust of the mundane world? The Dharma King made his vow as heavy as a mountain; the deluded child longs to return, shedding frequent tears.
If you can understand how to turn back and contemplate your own nature, the hundred-and-eight beads are all the treasures of your own house.
Gazing westward, the crimson clouds and the white sun’s orb; looking up, the precious throne and the body of purple-gold.

One realm is pure, and every realm is pure; ten recitations are sincere, and every thought is true. Born into the city of Ultimate Bliss, one shall never fall back; throughout the entirety of space, there is not a speck of dust.
Having previously floated and sunk within the sea of suffering, how fortunate I am now to be one who has reached the other shore!
Those born in this Sahā world are utterly deluded; ensnared by manifold sufferings, they lack the thought of liberation. While in this life, they possess no further pure karma;

how then could there be a time of escape at the moment of death? Though the hundreds of thousands of sūtras constantly offer such exhortations, among billions of people, only one or two understand them.
O Great Sage with golden arms, hold me dear and quickly lead me into the lotus pond!
The Eulogy by Master Lingfeng says:
I bow my head to the Great Teacher Chushi, who is none other than Amitābha, the Perfectly Awakened One. By means of these subtle and wondrous gāthās, may I be inspired to recite and study them.
With one reading and a second, the thoughts of worldly dust shall vanish; with a third and a fourth, defilements [shall be purified].
This brief composition has been read one hundred, ten thousand, a million, or even ten million times; this body has already been entrusted to the lotus.

I also pray that all future readers and reciters, like me, shall ultimately be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. May it further gather in boundless practitioners of *nien-fo*, forever shattering the evil of bifurcating phenomena from principle.
Because they dwell together in purity, the four are pure as one; this is a method that is perfectly integrated, direct, and transcendent.
The Pure Land Dharma Words of Master Youxi:
His Dharma Heir Zhengzhi.

Regarding the methods for practicing cultivation, these are the excellent medicine for verifying realization according to the Tathāgata. As medicine expands to meet the breadth of illnesses, their number exceeds that of the sands of the Ganges.
O Śāriputra, if one seeks the most direct path and the most essential method, none is better than reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land;
this may be called the secret formula for swiftly attaining the path of enlightenment. Indeed, escaping the cycle of birth and death relies upon three powers: first, the power of self-effort.

Second is the power of others; third is the power of innate merit. If one strives solely to awaken to and clarify the mind-ground, to tear asunder the net of ignorance, and to emerge from the river of craving and desire—whether becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch—this is called "self-power.

Such individuals are immeasurable heroes and true great beings (*mahāsattva*). They include the various great Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and great ancestral masters throughout the Buddha’s lifetime and during the period of the True Dharma.
Such people, in this age of the Dharma’s decline, possess inferior faculties; though they may practice, they do not awaken, and though they awaken, they lack refinement.
Their internal illumination seems to suggest liberation, yet they remain deluded when confronted with external objects. Even if they were not deluded, they would still be like unbaked earthenware.

For Bodhisattvas there is the darkness of being separated from their physical bodies, and for those who have attained the first fruit of the path, there is the obscurity of entering the womb; compared to these, how can ordinary beings avoid drifting along with the current?
The futility of self-reliance and the ineffectiveness of efforts to transcend the mundane world lead to error after error, which is truly heart-wrenching.

For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have compassionately bestowed expedient means, providing Dharma-gates that rely upon others. These Dharma-gates are numerous in both sutras and treatises;

yet when one seeks those that offer earnest, heartfelt exhortations and express the highest praise, they are found in the teachings of the Great Patriarchs, whose profound influence has inspired the veneration of the human mind.
I respectfully submit this. I hold that the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the ultimate path. Every word elucidates the Pure Land as being solely mind;
every phrase expounds the original nature of Amitābha. Those who awaken to this realize that the mind of birth-and-death and the Buddha-mind are equal.

The mind-land and the Buddha-land are without difference; those who cultivate this attain wondrous contemplation that accords with the wondrous realm, wherein self-power and other-power are complemented.
How much more so for the power of inherently existing merit and the beginningless, intrinsically endowed nature!

Thus, that which has been fully manifested through kalpas of accumulation suddenly erupts by means of this, whereby the retribution of the Sahā world is fulfilled and the Pure Land appears before one.
They are born through transformation within lotus flowers; they are not deluded by the aggregates of birth. Once entered, they enter forever, never again to regress.
Therefore, those who are born there are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). Their number is exceedingly great.

Compared to those who have entered the Path while remaining in the Sahā world—where coarse and powerful sensory objects, perilous difficulties, and evil paths exist everywhere—the former certainly cannot be equated with the latter. Nevertheless, it is not difficult to speak of this, but to practice it...
To aspire [to rebirth] is difficult; to practice it is not difficult; for the mind alone is what is difficult. This was the admonition of those of old, which we should follow.
Yang Cigong said: "If attachment is not deep, one will not be born in Saṃsāra; if mindfulness is not single-minded, one will not be born in Sukhāvatī.

Now, to recite the Buddha’s name with a unified mind, earnestly holding the name with a focused and undistracted resolve, is indeed sublime. However, there may be times when one forgets and is unable [to maintain this].
Moment by moment, one cannot remain free from the entanglements of emotional attachment;

indeed, it is only by treating such attachment lightly that one may eliminate its delusions, sever the root of emotion, and escape the net of craving—this is the sublime path. Yet, there are those who can contemplate this but cannot forget it, or who have forgotten it but cannot exhaust it;
this is for no other reason than that their minds lack single-mindedness. In this Sahā world, if there is even a single instance where love is not treated lightly, then...
If one is drawn away at the moment of death by this single attachment, how much more so when there are many attachments?

If one is turned by this single thought at the moment of death due to a lack of single-mindedness toward the Pure Land, how much more so when there are many thoughts? Indeed, attachments may be slight, moderate, or profound.

There is the retribution of the body (*vipāka-phala*), and there is the circumstantial retribution (*niṣyanda-phala*). To enumerate their categories exhaustively: parents, wives, children; brothers, friends; fame, achievement, wealth, and honor;
essays, prose, and verse; the Way, arts, and crafts; clothing, food, and drink; houses, fields, and gardens; forests, springs, flowers, and fruits;
precious jewels and objects of play—these are too numerous to list. Some are as vast and heavy as Mount Tai, while others are minute.
Yet it is lighter than a goose feather. To have even one thing not forgotten is love; to have even one thought not omitted is love.
If there is one love remaining in the breast, then thoughts will not be unified; if there is one thought that does not return to oneness, then rebirth cannot occur.
Alas! If love is not profound, one is not born in Saṃsāra; if thoughts are not unified, one is not born in Sukhāvatī. These two—
These words are the golden probe for scraping away cataracts from the eyes and the sacred medicine for curing ailments of the vital organs.

All who are resolved to seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss should inscribe them upon the walls of their dwellings and engrave them upon their skin. They should recite them with solemnity at all times and maintain mindfulness of them in every thought.

Day by day, they should strive to diminish their attachment to this Sahā world; day by day, they should strive to unify their thoughts upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss—lightening it further and further.
By this, one gradually ascends toward the Unconditioned (*nirvāṇa*). One after another, one gradually approaches the Ultimate.

If one can truly do so, although one has not yet escaped the *apāya* realms, one is no longer a long-term guest in Saṃsāra; though one has not yet been born in the Precious Abode, one is already a distinguished guest of Sukhāvatī.
When the right mindfulness manifests at the moment of death, rebirth in Sukhāvatī is certain. Someone asked: "What of those with light attachments?"

Because it is without marks and yet Real, all phenomena—the environment and its inhabitants, form and mind, self and others, ordinary beings and sages—of the ten directions and the three periods of time, all manifest vividly and simultaneously within the present single thought-moment of my own mind that is without marks and Real. Now, for the sake of the great assembly, I shall speak of them briefly. There are eight such aspects, namely: the deviant and the correct, the true and the false, the great and the small, and the partial and the universal.
"Perfect" refers to this. What are meant by the terms "deviant and correct," "true and false," "great and small," "partial and perfect"?

In the world there are practitioners who practice exclusively in a one-sided manner, failing to investigate their own minds and knowing only external affairs; they may seek profit and offerings, or crave fame and reputation.
If one generates the mind [of awakening] out of greed for the pleasures of the present life, or with the hope for future karmic rewards, such a resolve is called "perverse.
Since it seeks neither gain and fame nor the fruits of sensual pleasure and reward, but aims solely at [transcending] birth and death for the sake of Bodhi, such a resolve is called "correct.
Moment by moment, one seeks the Buddha-way above; thought after thought, one transforms sentient beings below.

Upon hearing that the path of the Buddha is long and distant, one does not give rise to retreat or cowardice; observing that sentient beings are difficult to deliver, one does not give rise to weariness or aversion.
It is like ascending a mountain ten thousand fathoms high—one must reach its summit; or like climbing a nine-storied pagoda—one must reach its peak.

To resolve the mind in this way is called "true. If one has transgressions yet does not repent them, or faults yet does not eliminate them, being turbid within while appearing pure without—this is merely the beginning.
Diligence ends in indolence. Though one may have good intentions, they are mostly intermingled with fame and profit; though one possesses wholesome dharmas, they are further defiled by sinful karma.
A resolve made in such a manner is called "false. Only when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted will my vow be exhausted;
only when the path to enlightenment is accomplished will my vow be fulfilled. A resolve made in such a manner is called "great. Contemplate this.
To regard the three realms as a prison and the cycle of birth and death as an enemy, aspiring only to deliver oneself while having no desire to deliver others—such a resolve is called "small.

If one perceives that there are sentient beings and a Buddha-way external to the mind, vowing to deliver them and achieve enlightenment, yet not forgetting one's own merit and not extinguishing one's own knowledge and vision—such a resolve is called "partial. If...
Knowing that the self-nature is sentient beings, one vows to deliver them. Knowing that the self-nature is the Buddha-way, one vows to achieve it.
One does not perceive even a single dharma as existing apart from the mind.

With a mind like space, one makes a vow like space, practices a conduct like space, and realizes a fruit like space; yet, even the mark of space cannot be apprehended. To resolve the mind in this manner is called...
This constitutes its circularity. To know these eight kinds of distinctions is to know critical examination; to know critical examination is to know what to reject and what to adopt;

and to know what to reject and what to adopt is to be able to generate the resolve for enlightenment. How does one conduct this critical examination? It means: regarding the resolve I have generated, among these eight [types]...
Is it deviant or correct? Is it true or false? Is it great or small? Is it partial or complete? How should one reject or accept? That is to say:
one rejects the deviant, the false, the small, and the partial; one accepts the correct, the true, the great, and the complete.
Only by generating the mind in this way can it be called the genuine generation of the bodhicitta. Among all virtues, this bodhicitta—
"O King, there must be specific causes and conditions for such a thought to arise. Briefly stated, there are ten kinds of causes and conditions. What are these ten?
First, because one recollects the profound kindness of the Buddha; second, because one recollects the kindness of one's parents;

third, because one recollects the kindness of teachers and elders; fourth, because one recollects the kindness of donors; fifth, because one recollects the kindness of sentient beings; sixth, because one recollects death..."
Because birth is suffering; seventh, because of honoring one’s own spiritual nature; eighth, because of repenting karmic obstructions; ninth, because of seeking rebirth in a pure land;
and tenth, for the sake of mindfulness so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. What is meant by "mindfulness of the Buddha’s profound kindness"?

It is said that I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, first resolved to attain enlightenment for the sake of beings such as ourselves, practicing the bodhisattva path through immeasurable kalpas and undergoing all manner of sufferings.
When I was creating karma, the Buddha felt compassion and sought to teach and transform me through skillful means;

yet, out of my own ignorance, I did not know how to believe or accept his guidance. Consequently, I fell into hell, where the Buddha again felt profound sorrow, wishing to take my suffering upon himself; however, I—
My karma is heavy; I cannot save myself. Having been born into the human realm, the Buddha used skillful means to cause me to plant roots of goodness.
From life to life and birth to birth, he has followed me, never abandoning me for even a moment. When the Buddha first appeared in the world, I was still submerged in the depths of saṃsāra.

Now that I have obtained a human body, the Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa. By what sin am I born in this age of the Dharma’s decline? By what merit am I permitted to enter the monastic order? What obstacles...
Yet I did not behold the Golden Body; how fortunate that I have personally encountered the śarīra. Reflecting thus, I thought:
had I not planted roots of goodness, how could I have heard the Buddha-dharma? Had I not heard the Buddha-dharma, how could I have known that I constantly receive the Buddha’s grace?

This grace and this virtue are as difficult to describe as a mountain or a heap. Were it not for the arousal of a vast mind, the practice of the bodhisattva path, and the establishment of the Buddha-dharma, [this would not be so].
To save and deliver sentient beings, even if one were to grind one's bones to powder and crush one's body to dust, how could one ever repay them?
This is the first causal condition for generating the bodhicitta. How does one contemplate the kindness of one’s parents? Alas, alas, my parents! Their toil in bringing me forth was immense.

For ten months and three years, they carried me in the womb and nursed me with milk; they pushed aside the dry to give me the moist and swallowed the bitter to spit out the sweet. Only then did I attain human form. [They] pointed...

We hope that [the family] will continue the ancestral tradition and maintain the ancestral sacrifices. Now that we have already left the household life, we falsely claim the title of Śākyaputra and shamefully bear the name of śramaṇa;
yet we do not provide them with fine food, nor do we provide for their sacrificial rites and tomb-sweeping.
We cannot nourish their physical bodies while they are alive, nor can we guide their spirits after death. This is a great loss to the world and offers no real benefit to the transcendental realm.

Since both paths have been lost, grave offenses are difficult to escape. Reflecting thus, one realizes that only by constantly practicing the Buddha-way throughout hundreds and thousands of lifetimes across ten directions and three periods of time, universally delivering all sentient beings, can not only the parents of this single life, but the parents of every lifetime, all receive deliverance;
and not only the parents of this single person, but the parents of every person, all be enabled to transcend and ascend. This is...
This is the second causal condition for generating the bodhicitta. What is meant by "recalling the kindness of one's teachers"?

Although parents are able to give birth to and raise one’s body, if there were no worldly teachers, one would not know propriety and righteousness; if there were no supramundane teachers, one would not understand the Buddha-dharma.
If one does not know propriety and righteousness, one is the same as the various species of animals; if one does not understand the Buddha-dharma, then...

How are we any different from worldly people? Now, we have a rudimentary knowledge of propriety and righteousness and a basic understanding of the Buddha-dharma. The *kāṣāya* robe covers our bodies and the precepts permeate us.
This profound grace was obtained from our teachers and elders. If we were to seek only the minor fruits [of the Śrāvaka path], we could merely benefit ourselves;
but now, for the sake of the Mahāyāna, we universally vow to benefit others, whereby both types of teachers—those of this world and those of the supramundane—shall alike receive our benefit.
This is the third cause and condition for generating the bodhicitta. What is meant by "mindfulness of the benefactor's kindness"?

It means that all the provisions we use daily are not our own; the morning and evening meals throughout the three periods of the day, the clothing for the four seasons, what is required during illness, and all expenditures for body and speech—all of these originate from the power of others, which we employ as our own.
Therefore, we must exert ourselves to the utmost in following their will.
They till the soil with their own hands, yet it is still difficult to sustain themselves; I, however, sit at ease while receiving food, yet even this does not satisfy my heart.
They spin and weave without ceasing, yet they still find it arduous; I, however, wear clothing with abundance, never knowing how to cherish or economize it.

They live in huts with doors of woven branches and thatched roofs, struggling in turmoil for the rest of their lives; I, however, dwell in spacious halls and quiet courtyards, passing the year in leisurely ease. While they labor thus...
To provide for my comfort and find peace of mind—using the benefit of others to nourish one's own person—is this not contrary to reason?

Unless one possesses the dual movement of compassion and wisdom and the twin adornments of merit and insight, such that donors and believers receive grace and sentient beings receive gifts, then even a grain of rice or a thread of silk will result in a debt that must be repaid, and an evil retribution will be difficult to escape.
This is the fourth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta.

What is meant by "mindfulness of the kindness of sentient beings"? It means that from beginningless kalpas, throughout life after life, I and all sentient beings have alternately served as parents to one another;

thus, we have all been indebted to each other. Although we are now separated by lifetimes and, in our delusion, do not recognize one another, when we reason according to this principle, how could there not be a way to repay their kindness?
How can we know that those who now wear fur and carry horns were not once our own children? Now...

Among these wriggling and flying creatures, who knows that they have not once been my own father? Whenever one sees those who were separated from their parents in childhood, by the time they reach adulthood, even their features are entirely forgotten;
how much more so for karmic relatives from past lives, whose names and clans are now impossible to recall.
Yet they are crying out beneath the hells and wallowing amidst the hungry ghosts; who knows their agony, and how can they endure their hunger and emptiness?
I submit this appeal: although I have neither seen nor heard it myself, that person must surely seek rescue and salvation. It is not possible to set forth such a matter except through the Sūtras;
it is not possible to utter such words except through the Buddha. How could those people of wrong views be sufficient to know this?
Therefore, the Bodhisattva regards even ants as having all been his parents in the past and as future Buddhas; he constantly contemplates their benefit and reflects upon how to repay their kindness.
This kindness constitutes the fifth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta. What is meant by "recalling the suffering of birth and death"?
It means that I and all sentient beings have, since time immemorial, constantly remained within birth and death without attaining liberation, whether in the human realm or the heavens.

In this realm and other directions, there are ten thousand modes of emergence and disappearance; in a mere moment, one ascends or sinks. Suddenly one is a celestial being, suddenly a human, and suddenly a denizen of hell, an animal, or a hungry ghost.
One leaves the black gates in the morning and returns by evening; one briefly departs from the iron caves only to enter them again.

The wardens of hell grow weary from their constant toil—who would believe the instructions of Lord Yama?

When experiencing [retribution], one knows the pain, yet though one regrets it, how can it be undone? Once released, one forgets again, and one’s karmic actions remain as they were before. They are whipped...
When a donkey bleeds, who knows the grief of its mother? When a pig is led to the slaughter, how can it recognize the pain of its sire?
To eat one’s own offspring without realizing it—even King Wen was like this; to devour one’s own kin without awareness—such is the nature of all beings.
Those once bound by affection have now become enemies; those who were former foes have now become flesh and blood. She who was once my mother...
To become a wife—to take as a husband one who was formerly a father—is something known through past karma; it is shameful and disgraceful.
To those with the divine eye, it is both laughable and pitiable. Having been carried for ten months amidst a mass of filth, she emerges at once from the path of pus and blood;

Desire arises; in an instant, old age and sickness follow one after another. Swiftly, impermanence arrives.
Wind and fire sear and torment within, causing the consciousness to become disordered and chaotic. Vital essence and blood are exhausted; skin and flesh wither from the outside.
Not a single hair is not pierced by needles; every orifice is as if cut by a blade. Like a tortoise about to be cooked, it struggles to shed its shell.
It is as easy as this; yet when the spirit seeks to depart, its leaving the body is doubly difficult. The mind has no permanent master;
it is like a merchant, rushing to and fro from place to place. The body has no fixed form; it is like a house, frequently moving from one location to another.

The dust motes of the great trichiliocosm cannot exhaust the count of bodies that have come and gone; who can calculate the waves of tears shed in parting across the four seas? Lofty and vast [is the accumulation]...
Bones. Beyond those lofty mountains, there lie vast stretches of corpses more numerous than the earth itself. Had one not heard the Buddha’s words, who would have seen or heard of such things?
Had one not beheld the Buddhist scriptures, how could one know or awaken to this truth?

If one continues to harbor attachments as before and remains mired in delusion as of old, I fear that throughout ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, one will err once and err a hundred times. For a human body is difficult to obtain.
Things are easily lost. Good times pass away with ease and are difficult to pursue again. The road ahead is dark and shrouded; partings shall be long and enduring.

The retributions of the three evil realms must be endured by oneself alone; the pain is beyond words. Who can take one’s place? To bring such thoughts to mind—how could one not feel a chill in the heart?
Therefore, one ought to sever the stream of birth and death and emerge from the sea of craving and desire, so that self and others may both be saved, and together reach the other shore.
Ascending [to the Way], the extraordinary merit of kalpas beyond measure rests upon this single act; this is the sixth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta.
What is meant by "honoring one's own spirit"? It means that my present single-mindedness is, directly and immediately, non-dual and indistinguishable from Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Why is it that while the World-Honored One attained perfect enlightenment long ago after immeasurable kalpas, we remain in a state of delusion?

Due to such perversions, we remain mere ordinary beings. Furthermore, while the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is adorned with immeasurable supernatural powers, wisdom, and meritorious virtues, we are bound only by immeasurable karmic fetters, afflictions, and the entanglements of birth and death.

Though the nature of the mind is one and the same, the difference between delusion and awakening is as vast as heaven and abyss. Reflecting quietly upon this, how can it not be a cause for shame? It is like a priceless jewel [lying hidden].

The jewel has sunk into the mud; it is regarded as mere rubble and not treated with love or respect. Therefore, one ought to use immeasurable wholesome dharmas to counteract the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Humanity’s path of progress is pointed toward by thousands of sutras and myriad treatises everywhere; for practice in the Dharma-ending age, nothing surpasses this.
Yet the sutras state that few good deeds do not arise, but it is through much merit that one attains [the goal]. Regarding "much merit," there is nothing better than upholding the Name.

Regarding the abundance of merit, nothing compares to giving rise to the vast and great mind (*mahācitta*). Therefore, even a momentary holding of the Holy Name surpasses a hundred years of practicing generosity;
a single arousal of the great mind exceeds eons of cultivation. For the original purpose of recollecting the Buddha is to become a Buddha oneself.

If the great mind is not aroused, what is the use of recollection? The arousal of the mind is fundamentally for the sake of cultivation; if one is not born in the Pure Land, then even [if one has cultivated], what is the use?

It is easy to generate [the aspiration] but difficult to maintain it. This constitutes planting the seed of Bodhicitta: one plows with the plow of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), and the fruit of the Path naturally increases.
Boarding the ship of great vows, one enters the ocean of the Pure Land; rebirth in the Western Quarter is certain. This is the ninth causal condition for generating the Bodhicitta.
