With causes perfected and fruits fulfilled, you have thus attained Buddhahood. Since becoming a Buddha, your transformative work has been completed and you have entered Nirvana.

Both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have already been extinguished, and only the Final Dharma remains. There are teachings but no people to uphold them; the heterodox and the orthodox are no longer distinguished. This is...
It is not that there is no discernment; rather, people compete for "self" and "other," and all pursue profit and fame. Looking around, this is the prevailing trend throughout the world.
They do not know who the Buddha is, what the Dharma means, or what the Sangha signifies.

To have declined to such a state is almost beyond words; whenever I think of it, tears involuntarily fall. As a son of the Buddha, I am unable to repay his kindness, and within me there is no benefit.
To myself, I have been of no benefit; externally, I have benefited no one; in life, I have been of no use to the times; and in death, I shall be of no use to those who come after.
Though heaven is high, it cannot cover me; though earth is thick, it cannot support me. Among those who commit the most grievous sins, who am I if not this person?
Because of this, my pain was unbearable and I saw no way out. Suddenly forgetting my own vulgarity and baseness, I abruptly gave rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*). Although I am unable—
At this time, we must turn back the final age; in the future, we shall surely strive to protect and uphold the True Dharma.
For this reason, together with various virtuous friends, we have come to this place of practice to offer repentance and establish this Dharma assembly.

We have made forty-eight great vows, vowing in each vow to deliver sentient beings, and harboring a profound resolve for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, aspiring in every thought to become Buddhas. From this moment on...
Day by day, until the end of the future, exhausting this single lifetime, I vow to return to An-yang (Sukhāvatī) and immediately ascend to the ninth grade.

Thereafter, I shall return to enter Saṃbhava (Sahā), so that the sun of the Buddha may shine once more, the Dharma-gate may be proclaimed again, and the ocean of the Sangha may be made clear within this realm;
so that the people may be transformed in the East, the eons may be further extended, and the True Dharma may abide for a long time. This is the... [region].
To distinguish the sincere and diligent efforts of the heart is the tenth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta.
When these ten conditions are fully understood and the eight dharmas are thoroughly known, one will then proceed toward the Gate of Existence and find the ground for its development.

Having together obtained this human body, dwelling in the Central Kingdom (Huaxia), with the six sense faculties unimpaired and the four elements in a state of light ease, and possessing faith, one is fortunately free from demonic interference.

How much more so now that we have been able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, encounter a site of enlightenment, hear the Buddha-dharma, behold the śarīra, practice the methods of repentance, meet virtuous friends, and possess such superior conditions?
If we do not give rise to this great resolve today, what day shall we wait for? I only pray that the great assembly will take pity on my foolish sincerity and have compassion for my suffering.
Aspire! Together establish this vow and together give rise to this mind. Let those who have not yet given rise to it do so now; let those who have already given rise to it cause it to increase;
and let those who have already increased it now continue it uninterruptedly. Do not shrink back out of fear of difficulty; do not be frivolous by regarding it as easy;
do not seek haste and lack long-term persistence; do not be indolent and lack vigor; and do not be despondent and fail to exert yourself.
Do not remain complacent and wait for the future; do not be consistently indifferent due to dullness and ignorance;
do not disparage yourself as being unworthy because your roots are shallow. It is like planting a tree: as time passes, though the roots were initially shallow, they grow deeper by the day.

It is also like sharpening a blade: through long use of the whetstone, even a dull blade becomes keen. How could one refrain from planting simply because the ground is shallow, allowing the tree to wither away on its own? Because...
Do not grind what is dull; set it aside as useless. Furthermore, if you consider spiritual practice to be suffering, you do not realize that indolence is even more bitter.

Through practice, one exerts effort for a brief time to attain peace and joy for eternal kalpas; through indolence, one seeks a fleeting ease for this single lifetime only to suffer for many lifetimes to come.
Moreover, if one takes the Pure Land as a vessel for crossing over, why worry about falling back? Furthermore, one attains non-arising.
If one possesses the power of patience, what need is there to worry about hardships? One should know that even the sinners in the hells gave rise to the aspiration for Bodhi in past kalpas;
how much more so should we, as human beings and sons of the Buddha, not establish great vows in this present life?

Though the beginningless delusion of the past cannot be remedied, now that we have attained awakening, the future can still be pursued. Yet, while we remain lost and have not yet awakened, it is certainly [the case that...]
How pitiable! If one knows [the truth] yet fails to practice it, this is all the more cause for lamentation. If one fears the suffering of hell, diligence will arise spontaneously;
if one contemplates the swiftness of impermanence, indolence will not arise.

Furthermore, one must take the Buddha-dharma as one's whip and virtuous friends as one's guides, never parting from them even in moments of haste and relying upon them for the rest of one's life; then there shall be no falling away.
Be cautious! Do not say that a single thought is trivial; do not claim that a sincere vow is of no benefit. If the mind is true, the reality will manifest;
if the vow is vast, the practice will be profound. Space is not the greatest; the sovereign mind is the greatest. The diamond is not the most solid; the power of the vow is the most solid.
If the great assembly can truly not reject my words, then the kinship of Bodhi shall be joined from this day forth, and the spiritual alliance of the Lotus Society shall be cemented from now on.
May we all aspire to be born together in the Pure Land, to behold Amitābha together, to transform sentient beings together, and to achieve perfect enlightenment together.
Who then knows that the thirty-two marks and the adornment of a hundred blessings in the future may not originate from this very day?
It begins with the arousal of the mind and the establishment of vows; may you and the great assembly strive together toward this—how fortunate, how fortunate!
In a letter to the layman Mao Jingyuan, it was said: "That you have completed the construction of the bridge may be called a most magnificent achievement."
However, the mind of a layperson delights in goodness without weariness; as soon as one good deed is completed, another is undertaken.

While this is indeed praiseworthy, what does it avail regarding the great matter of birth and death? If one does not regard the great matter of birth and death as urgent, yet busies oneself with doing good—so that the virtuous deeds performed are like Mount Sumeru—they are all merely karmic conditions for birth and death. When will there ever be an end to them? Goodness!
As affairs multiply, birth and death become ever more vast. A single thought of attachment binds one for ten thousand kalpas; is this not something to be feared?
Layman, you have long since penetrated the public cases of the world and have long practiced the pure karma of the Western Paradise. Yet, your resolve regarding birth and death is not urgent;
you cannot cast off domestic ties; you cannot decline the entreaties of human relations; and your mind in reciting the Buddha’s name is not single-minded. Why is this?
Is it that the sense-faculties have not been severed? Or is it that you are entangled by craving and attachment? Regarding these two matters, you should conduct a careful examination.
If you do not decisively sever all domestic concerns and worldly affairs with a single stroke, you must exert all your strength to uphold the six characters of the Great Name.
To desire liberation from this Sahā world and rebirth in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) is difficult.

To desire liberation from birth and death without being born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, and to desire to avoid falling into the lower realms without escaping birth and death—this is even more difficult.
Even if one does not lose the human body for one or two lifetimes, what can that possibly accomplish? Alas! Layman, your wisdom-mind is so clear and sharp; yet regarding your family affairs...

With such abundance, with such capable descendants, and with every affair to one’s satisfaction, if one still cannot let go of myriad concerns to single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name—is this to be seen as Heaven betraying man, or man betraying Heaven?

One does not regard the recitation of the Buddha’s name as urgent, but instead regards minor worldly virtues as urgent; one does not prioritize the great matter of birth and death, but instead prioritizes [worldly] people...
To prioritize the karmic rewards of the heavens is to be ignorant of what comes first and what comes last.

For a lay practitioner today, the primary task is to decline all social obligations and focus the mind single-mindedly on the Buddha’s name. To further this with the practice of fasting and precepts would be the height of excellence.

Generally speaking, the Western Land of Buddhas cannot be reached through indolent or scattered virtues; nor can the cycle of birth and death across ten thousand kalpas be overcome through complacency or negligence.
That which can liberate us is impermanent and swift; morning and evening it arrives. How can one not prepare for it early?
Among those I know, there are very few; among those I know, there are even fewer with whom one may discuss this matter.
Setting aside one layman, who is it that holds such deep expectations? If you do not discard the words because of the person, I would be grateful for your diligent effort.
If you say, "I am unable," then there is nothing that can be done.
The Dharma Words on the Buddha-Recitation Method by Chan Master Che-wu, compiled by his Dharma-heir Liaoliang:
"The single thought-moment of our present existence is entirely true and yet entirely deluded; entirely deluded and yet entirely true—it never changes throughout the day."
Throughout the day, one follows conditions. Now, if one does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm while recollecting the Buddha-realm, one will instead recollect the nine realms.
If one does not recollect the Three Vehicles, one will recollect the six classes of ordinary beings. If one does not recollect humans and devas, one will recollect the three miserable paths.

If one does not recollect ghosts and animals, one will recollect hell. This is because as long as one possesses a mind, it is impossible to be without thought. Only the Buddha alone possesses the essence of the mind that is free from thought.
From the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) down to the lower realms, all possess thought. Whenever a single thought arises, it necessarily falls within the ten realms.
There is no thought that exists outside of the ten realms, for there is nothing external to the ten dharma-realms.
Every arising of a single thought serves as the condition for one birth. If one understands this principle, it is impossible not to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name. If this mind...

To be able to accord with the merit of the primary and secondary marks, as well as the great name of myriad virtues, through the power of equal great kindness and great compassion, is precisely the mindfulness of the Dharma-realm of the Buddhas.
To be able to accord with the bodhicitta and the myriad practices of the six pāramitās is precisely the mindfulness of the Dharma-realm of the Bodhisattvas.
To accord with the twelve links of dependent origination by means of a selfless mind is precisely the mindfulness of the Dharma-realm of the Pratyekabuddhas.
It is the realm (*dhātu*). When one observes the Four Truths with a mind free from self, that is the mindfulness of the *śrāvaka* dharma-realm.

If it is associated with the four *dhyānas*, the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), and the superior grade of the ten wholesome actions, that is the mindfulness of the celestial dharma-realm.

If it is associated with the five precepts, that is the mindfulness of the human dharma-realm. If one cultivates dharmas such as the precepts and wholesome deeds while simultaneously harboring anger, pride, or arrogance—

If one acts with a resentful mind, one falls into the dharma-realm of the asuras. If one contemplates the ten evil deeds of the lower grade with a lax and gentle mind, one falls into the dharma-realm of animals.
If one acts with a mind that is half-lax and half-urgent in conjunction with the ten evil deeds of the middle grade, one falls into the dharma-realm of hungry ghosts.
If one acts with a fierce and blazing mind in conjunction with the ten evil deeds of the upper grade, one falls into hell.

The realm of hell is the dharma-realm of the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*). These are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct; false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech;
as well as covetousness, malice, and wrong views. To act contrary to these constitutes the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). You should examine yourself in secret:

among the thoughts that arise in your daily life, with which realm do they most frequently correspond, and with which realm do they most intensely correspond? This will determine where you shall find refuge in days to come.
As for the place where one establishes one's destiny, there is no need to ask others.
Truly regarding birth and death, one should resolve to attain Bodhicitta and, with deep faith and aspiration, hold the Buddha’s name.

These sixteen characters constitute the great fundamental principle of the Dharma-gate of Nianfo. If the mind that truly regards birth and death does not arise, all [other teachings] are... [omitted].
All these are shown to be mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*). Among all the heavy sufferings of the world, none exceeds birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Without understanding birth and death, one dies in birth and is born from death; life follows death, and death follows life. Emerging from one womb and entering another, casting off one skin-sack and taking up another, the suffering is already unbearable;
how much more so for those who have not yet escaped the cycle of rebirth, where one cannot avoid falling into the wombs of pigs or dogs?
There is no womb they will not penetrate; there is no donkey skin bag or horse skin bag they will not take up.
This human body is most difficult to obtain and most easily lost. A single moment’s lapse of thought, and one enters the evil realms. The three paths are easy to enter but difficult to leave;
the duration in hell is long and the suffering is heavy. Since the time of the Seven Buddhas, we have been as mere ants for eighty thousand [great kalpas].

Even after the passing of kalpas, they have not yet escaped their pigeon bodies; their time in the animal realm has already reached its extreme limit, while their time in the hells and as hungry ghosts is twice as long.

Having endured these long kalpas for so long, when will it ever end? When will there be rest? Tormented by myriad sufferings, with no refuge and no savior—every time I speak of this, my body hairs stand on end;
every time I give rise to a single thought of it, my five viscera feel as if they are being burned. Therefore, I now painfully contemplate birth and death as if I had lost [a beloved one].
Regarding my parents, it is as if one were trying to extinguish a fire on one's head. Now, while I am subject to birth and death, I seek liberation;

yet all sentient beings likewise dwell within birth and death and should all likewise seek liberation. They and I are originally of one and the same essence, and they have all been my parents throughout many lifetimes.
If I do not contemplate their universal deliverance but seek only my own benefit, it would be contrary to reason.
Where there is deficiency, the mind remains unsettled; how much more so when the great resolve is not awakened? Then, externally, one cannot communicate with the Buddhas;
internally, one cannot harmonize with one's original nature; above, one cannot perfectly fulfill the Buddha-way; and below, one cannot extensively benefit all sentient beings.

How can one be liberated from the beginningless bonds of affection? How can one resolve the beginningless offenses of enmity? The karmic offenses accumulated over kalpas are difficult to expiate through repentance;
the roots of goodness accumulated over kalpas are difficult to bring to maturity. In whatever practice one engages, there arise many obstacles and conditions.

Even if one were to achieve some realization, it would ultimately fall into the partial and inferior. Therefore, one must give rise to the great bodhicitta in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Once the great mind has been aroused, one should cultivate the great practices.
Among all the gateways of practice, there is none that is more easily undertaken, more easily accomplished, most secure, and most perfectly sudden than relying upon deep faith.

One should resolve to uphold the names of the Buddhas. That which is called "profound faith" is this: Śākyamuni Tathāgata certainly utters no deceptive words, and the World-Honored Amitābha certainly makes no empty vows.
Furthermore, by means of the cause of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth, one will necessarily attain the fruit of beholding the Buddha and being born in the Pure Land.

The cause is not discarded in vain, and the fruit is not obtained by chance. The *Wangsheng zhuan* (Biographies of Those Reborn) records the auspicious signs at the time of death, which appear in abundance.
The ranks stand in orderly rows. How could they deceive me? Having gained such conviction, my longing and joy become most earnest.

When I look back upon the suffering of this Sahā world by contrast with the bliss of that land, my revulsion and desire for departure grow profound, as if fleeing from a cesspool or escaping from a prison.

When I look afar at the bliss of that land by contrast with the suffering of this Sahā world, my delight and joy become most earnest, as if returning to one’s native home or rushing toward precious treasure.

In short, it is like one who is thirsty seeking a drink, hungry seeking food, afflicted by illness seeking a fine medicine, an infant seeking its compassionate mother, one pursued by an enemy with a drawn sword seeking to flee, or one fallen into water or fire urgently seeking rescue.
If you can be thus earnest, no external circumstances or conditions will be able to lead you astray. Thereafter...
With this mind of faith and aspiration, hold fast to the Name. Each single utterance is a seed of the Nine Lotus Worlds;

each single recitation is the primary cause for rebirth there. You must ensure that mind follows mind in succession and thought follows thought without deviation. Be exclusively focused and diligent, without distraction or interruption.
The longer you practice, the firmer it becomes; the more you recite, the more earnest you become. After a long, long time, it will naturally be accomplished.
This is a fragment. One enters into single-mindedness without distraction. Indeed, it is so.
If one were not to attain rebirth, then Śākyamuni Tathāgata would be a speaker of falsehood, and the World-Honored Amitābha would have made a vain vow. Could such a principle possibly exist?
Among all things in the world, nothing is more precious than the spirit; among all things in the world, nothing is more worthy of being cherished than time.
A single thought of purity is the causal condition for the fruit of Buddhahood; a single thought of defilement is the generative cause for the nine realms of existence.
Every movement of a single thought is a seed for the ten realms—how can one not cherish this? Once a day has passed, one's life is diminished accordingly.
A single inch of time is a single inch of the light of life; how can one not cherish it? If you know that the spirit is something to be treasured, do not squander it.
Instead, maintain the recitation of the Buddha’s name in every thought-moment so that your time is not spent in vain, and cultivate pure karma at every instant.
Should you set aside the Buddha’s name to instead practice the noble deeds of the three vehicles, this too is a waste.

The human spirit is like a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt; yet it is used to strike a mere field mouse. How much more so when one creates karma for the cycle of birth and death within the six realms of existence!
Should one set aside the practice of pure karma to instead pursue the provisional vehicles and their minor fruits, this too is merely to waste one's time in vain.
It is like using a wish-fulfilling jewel to trade for a single garment or a single meal; how much more so when it concerns attaining the tainted fruits of the human or celestial realms?

If one values [the Dharma] in this way and cherishes it in this way, then the mind will become focused and the Buddha will be easily invoked; practice will be diligent and karma will be easily refined.
Thus, one shall truly be born in the Pure Land, personally behold Amitābha, receive his instructions at that time, and face-to-face receive his compassionate [guidance].

As for Sound: he attained wondrous enlightenment regarding his own mind and profoundly realized the Dharma-realm. He could extend a single thought-moment into a long kalpa and condense a long kalpa into a single thought-moment.

Having achieved the perfect fusion of thought-moments and kalpas, he attained great sovereign mastery. Is this not the fruition of his own diligent practice, his own profound cherishing and careful cultivation?

Generally, one realizes the Way (*darśanamārga*) before cultivating it (*bhāvanāmārga*), and cultivates it before realizing its fruit (*adhigamamārga*). This is the common path of the thousand sages and an immutable principle established throughout the ages.
Yet, how easy is it to speak of "realizing the Way"? If following the *Śāsana-yāna* (the Vehicle of the Teachings), one must first develop a vast and perfect understanding;
if following the *Zongmen* (the School of the Lineage), one must directly penetrate the heavy barriers. Only then can one discuss the cultivation of the Way; otherwise, it is not so.
Those who practice blindly and train recklessly will inevitably collide with walls and strike against barriers, falling into pits and ravines.
Only the single gate of the Pure Land is not thus: beyond a hundred trillion Buddha-lands to the west, there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells and expounds the Dharma. Merely by making a vow and upholding His name, one [attains rebirth].
This is the realm of abiding and birth, known and seen directly by the Buddha’s mind and the Buddha’s eye;

it is not something that can be known or seen by the worthies and sages of the three vehicles. One should simply have deep faith in the Buddha’s words, and based upon this, make vows and hold the Name.
This means that one takes the Buddha’s knowledge and vision as one’s own knowledge and vision; there is no need to seek a separate gate of enlightenment elsewhere.

In other approaches to the cultivation of the Way, one must first attain awakening and then practice according to the Dharma: by gathering the mind, one achieves meditative concentration (*samādhi*); based on concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) arises; and based on wisdom, delusions (*kleśa*) are severed.
The wisdom thus produced varies in its degree of excellence, and the delusions severed vary in their depth. Only after this can one discuss the possibility of regression.

Regarding non-retrogression: only within this gate of the Pure Land, by means of the mind of faith and aspiration alone, single-mindedly upholding the Name until one reaches the state of "one-pointedness without distraction," does the pure karma become fully perfected.
After death, one will certainly attain rebirth there. Once rebirth is attained, one shall never again fall back.
Furthermore, regarding the cultivation of the Way through other gates, one must first repent for one's present karma; if [this] present karma...

If one does not repent, it will immediately obstruct the Path, leaving no way to advance in cultivation. Those who cultivate the practice of purity attain rebirth while still carrying their karmic burdens;

they do not need to repent for their karma, because a single utterance of the Buddha’s name with a sincere mind can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

Furthermore, in other gateways of the Path, one must sever the afflictions (*kleśa*); if even a fraction of the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *bhava-rāga*) has not been eliminated—

If [afflictions] are not exhausted, then birth-and-death in segmented portions (*paricchinna-janma-maraṇa*) will not be exhausted, and one will be unable to escape the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
Only by cultivating pure karma can one emerge horizontally from the triple world (*tridhātu*) without severing afflictions; thus, one proceeds from this common dwelling to that common dwelling.
Once born in that land, the root-stalk of birth-and-death is forever severed. Having been born in that land, one constantly beholds the Buddha at all times.
At that time, one hears the Dharma; clothing, food, and dwellings appear spontaneously, and the waters, birds, and forests all preach the Dharma.

While dwelling within this land, one horizontally perceives the three higher Pure Lands. There, all superior virtuous beings assemble in one place, perfectly realizing the three types of non-retrogression and attaining the rank of Buddha in a single lifetime.
Thus, through the single gate of the Pure Land, one first seeks and realizes awakening.
This gate does not require the subsequent arousal of wisdom, nor the repentance of karma, nor the severing of afflictions;
it is the ultimate in economy and the ultimate in directness. When one attains entry through it, it is the ultimate in vastness and the ultimate in finality.

Students should contemplate this with a meticulous mind and examine it in detail: by reciting a single Buddha-name without mixing in other conditions, and completing ten recitations, one suddenly transcends.
To lack faith in this for many kalpas is truly to be like wood or stone. To abandon this and practice something else is either madness or folly.

This single thought-moment before us arises through conditions yet lacks intrinsic nature; it is without intrinsic nature yet arises through conditions. If it does not give rise to the Buddha-realm, it gives rise to the nine realms.

If we consider arising through conditions while lacking intrinsic nature, then the Buddha and [sentient beings] are equal in the single emptiness. If we consider [arising through conditions] while lacking intrinsic nature...
Upon birth, the superiority and inferiority of the ten realms are vastly different. When King Aṅgida was nearing death, a fly-swatter man brushed his face with a whisk;
because of a single thought of anger, the king subsequently fell into the state of a venomous snake. A certain woman, while crossing a river, lost her grip and her son fell into the water;
because she reached out to pull him from the water, she drowned along with him. Yet, because of her compassionate heart, she attained rebirth in the heavens. Indeed, a single...

If one contemplates compassion while harboring anger, the distinction between gods and beasts will eventually be established. Thus, should one not be cautious regarding that single thought arising at the moment of death?
If one sincerely contemplates Amitābha with this very mind and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, will one not surely behold the Buddha and attain rebirth?
However, this single thought cannot be achieved through mere luck; it must be maintained with sincerity and cultivated through long-standing practice. This is...

Therefore, when we recite this single phrase of Amitābha a thousand times, ten thousand times, or even throughout our entire lives and years, it is none other than for the sake of making this one thought thoroughly matured.
If this one thought indeed becomes pure and matured, then at the moment of death there will be only this one thought and no other thoughts.
If the recitation is truly like this, and one does not see Amitābha, what else could one see?
If people do not attain birth in the Pure Land, where else will they be reborn? I fear only that we lack sufficient self-confidence.
The nature of the single thought-moment before us is fundamentally of the same substance as the Buddha’s. The Buddha has long since awakened to this, yet I remain deluded;
though the Buddha has awakened, there is no increase in him, and though I remain deluded, there is no decrease in me. Although the Buddha has no increase, because...
Because it accords with their nature, they experience the great joy of the Dharma; yet though I do not diminish, because it is contrary to their nature, they encounter extreme suffering.
Within this mind of identical essence, although the Buddha experiences the joy of the Dharma, through his great compassion of identical essence and his objectless great kindness, he acts for them.
In every thought-moment you remember me; in every thought-moment you gather and transform me.
Within this mind-nature of our shared essence, although I have encountered manifold sufferings, I did not know to look up and seek refuge in the Buddha, nor did I know to remember the Buddha.

Instead, I merely followed external objects to give rise to thoughts and pursued my emotions to create karma. Throughout vast eons, what [remedy] can there be for my various grave karmas—the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds?

One does not create [the causes for] the three miserable realms or the eight difficulties; what various great sufferings would one not undergo? To speak of this is shameful; to contemplate it is terrifying.

If you do not now further recite the Buddha’s name, but instead continue as before to bury your head in creating all manner of karma, and continue as before to receive all manner of suffering from the very beginning, will you not feel shame?
Will you not feel dread? For now, know that the Buddha possesses great compassion and...

Compassion: In every thought-moment, I am mindful of how [the Buddha] gathered and transformed me. Thus, I now feel a profound sense of gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness; for this reason, I should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

For one-directional, long kalpas, I have endured manifold sufferings in vain; desiring to escape from suffering, I should therefore practice mindfulness of the Buddha. Regarding karma already committed, there is nothing that can be done;
but regarding future karma, can it not be avoided? Thinking thus, I give rise to a mind of shame and remorse; for this reason, I should practice mindfulness of the Buddha.

One should practice the mindfulness of the Buddha. The nature of the mind is of one substance with the Buddha; since it is said to be inherently present, how could it not exist right now? It is merely lacking in awakening and realization.

Because one seeks to awaken to the nature of the mind, one should practice the mindfulness of the Buddha. Because one practices the mindfulness of the Buddha in order to seek awakening to the mind, the mindfulness of the Buddha must be earnest.

One should practice the mindfulness of the Buddha with a heart of shame and remorse; the mindfulness of the Buddha must be earnest. One should practice the mindfulness of the Buddha with a heart of dread and suffering; the mindfulness of the Buddha must be earnest. One should practice the mindfulness of the Buddha with a heart of gratitude...
Recite the Buddha’s name with a heart of gratitude. One must be earnest in reciting the Buddha’s name. If I do not recite the Buddha’s name, the Buddha still remembers me;
now that I am sincerely and earnestly reciting the Buddha’s name, the Buddha will surely remember me even more so.
To know the small while not knowing the great, and to see the near while not seeing the far—this is the common lot of sentient beings.
How is it that these beings do not recognize the great debt of gratitude Amitābha Buddha owes them?
Countless eons ago, before the presence of Lokeśvararāja Buddha, the Buddha universally made four vows for the sake of suffering sentient beings in this evil world.
Based on eighteen kinds of great vows, he practiced the bodhisattva path for many long kalpas.
He relinquished the position of a golden-wheel-turning monarch, his kingdom, cities, wife, and children, as well as his head, eyes, marrow, and brain—countless thousands of millions of times.

This was but a single practice among the ten thousand practices: the giving of internal and external wealth. Such is that which a person of patience cannot endure, and which a practitioner cannot [bear].
Practice. Perfecting the myriad practices, with power at its peak and merit fully purified, he adorns and completes the Pure Land and attains Buddhahood for himself.
He manifests infinite emanations to receive and guide sentient beings, employing skillful means to gather and transform them, so that they may now be born in that land.
Thus, as it is for one person, so it is for many; as it is for many, so it is for one. If one observes from the perspective of the multitude, the Buddha is then universal.
It is for the sake of all sentient beings. Yet, if one views it from the perspective of a single individual, the Buddha acts solely for me alone.
His great vows, which accord with the nature of reality, were made for my sake; his great practices over long kalpas were cultivated for my sake;
the four lands were purified and adorned for my sake; and the three bodies were perfected for my sake. Thus, he manifests his form in every instance to guide and receive me, appearing everywhere.
These manifested auspicious signs are all for my sake. When I create karma, the Buddha awakens me;
when I undergo suffering, the Buddha rescues me; when I take refuge, the Buddha accepts me; and when I practice the path...

The Buddha has bestowed his grace upon me. All that the Buddha does for me in these various ways is nothing other than his desire for me to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, his desire for me to attain rebirth in the Pure Land, his desire for me to be forever liberated from all suffering and extensively receive the joy of the Dharma, and his desire for me to successively transform and deliver all sentient beings until I finally reach the stage of the One Life Remaining before Buddhahood. Alas! The Buddha’s—
This profound kindness and weighty virtue cannot be compared even to that of one's parents; though heaven and earth are insufficient to illustrate their height and depth.
Had I not heard this instruction, how could I have known this meaning? Had I not read the Buddhist scriptures, how could I have understood this principle?

From this day forward, I already know it. I shall only do my utmost to cultivate with diligence, exhaust myself in repaying this grace through sincere devotion, and dedicate my very life to the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
What more need be said?

Faith, aspiration, and the holding of the Name are the most supreme expedient for swiftly escaping saṃsāra. Lingfeng said:
"If faith and aspiration are not genuine, then even if one’s mind is undisturbed, one will still not attain birth [in the Pure Land].

If faith and aspiration are fierce and keen, then even if one recites the Buddha’s name with a distracted mind, one will certainly attain birth. Chewu said: "Simply keep these two dharmas—faith and aspiration—constantly present in the mind. As...

A loyal minister who receives the secret edicts of a sagacious sovereign, and a filial son who receives the stern commands of a compassionate father—regardless of whether their thoughts are many or few—all constitute the primary cause for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Therefore, faith, aspiration, and the recitation of the Name are the essential core of practice; one must not neglect them.
This is the sole focus of *The Essential Readings of the Lotus School* compiled by Master Lianxi, which places exclusive emphasis on faith, aspiration, and the recitation of the Name.
This Dharma profoundly accords with the purport of the *Ekavyūha-samādhi*;
it not only enables sentient beings burdened by many obstacles to ascend directly to the stage of non-retrogression, but also allows those filled with doubt to believe and find courage.

It is truly a compassionate vessel for the sea of suffering and a sun of wisdom for the dark path. Furthermore, there is a preface in one chapter which [expounds] the thorough compassion of Śākyamuni. To fill...
The Great Vows of Samantabhadra, the essential framework of the Pure Land, and the wondrous secret of holding the Name are all comprehensively summarized within this single preface.
Not only are the words concise and the meaning complete, but it also leaves no residue of the profound purport of the Pure Land teachings.
Upon my first reading, my joy exceeded all expectations; it was like a pauper finding treasure, or like one in darkness finding a lamp. Although there are many treatises on the Pure Land...

It is like a mountain of accumulated texts; among them, there is no lack of those that raise concerns regarding medicinal taboos. Only this single work is highly relevant to the present age, being both perfect and beautiful.
It is as certain as an arrow hitting the string or medicine matching the ailment; it is titled "That Which Must Be Read. What further doubt could there be?
Please circulate it immediately to establish pure karmic conditions. The Master said: "I have erroneously compiled these various writings; what benefit would circulation bring? However—"
This was merely my own self-exhortation. Because [the requester] pressed me with persistent entreaty, I finally entrusted him with the task of collating and editing it for Qijue.
My hope is that all those of like mind will together read and study it, so that they may clearly understand its meaning, give rise to faith, and make vows to initiate sublime practice.

One will thus swiftly escape saṃsāra and forever attain the stage of non-retrogression; there is nothing that surpasses this. I respectfully add these few words as a postscript to mark my joy in the Dharma.
Written on the Wuchen year of the Tongzhi era at Da Huankui Monastery in Ning County by Yina Xinxi.
